# Sūrah Al-Baqarah (Chapter 2) — Verse-by-Verse Tafsir

## Introduction to the Sūrah

Al-Baqarah is the longest sūrah in the Qur'an and the first great body of Madinan instruction in the written Book. Its passages came across different moments of the new community's life, yet they form one sustained education. The sūrah moves from faith to worship, from memory to law, and from private conscience to public obligation. It addresses people who believe, people who reject faith, and people who hide rejection behind religious speech. It then turns at length to the Children of Israel, not to make their history a distant spectacle, but to show the new community how a people may receive revelation and still weaken its force through evasion, selective obedience, or argument. Its title comes from the command to slaughter a cow in verses 67–73. That episode gives the chapter a fitting name: a direct command becomes difficult when submission is replaced by delay, needless questions, and reluctance to act.

The sūrah answers the prayer that closes al-Fātiḥah. The worshipper has asked to be guided along the straight path; al-Baqarah opens by identifying the Book as guidance and then describes the people who can receive it. That connection governs the chapter. Guidance is not presented as information alone. It appears as belief in the unseen, prayer, generosity, patience, fasting, pilgrimage, just trade, careful debt, family responsibility, restraint in conflict, and repentance after failure. Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the Sacred House and ask for a messenger among their descendants. The direction of prayer changes toward that House, making bodily worship declare a community's covenant. The history of earlier revelation and the law of the present community therefore belong to one argument: God guides through truth received inwardly and obeyed in visible life.

Its legal range is unusually broad because the community being formed needed more than private counsel. The chapter treats food, retaliation, wills, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, divorce, nursing, spending, warfare, oaths, usury, contracts, witnesses, and secured loans. Yet law never becomes detached administration. Commands are repeatedly tied to mindfulness of God, the final return, mercy, and the danger of concealing truth. The longest verse in the Qur'an records a debt so that memory and power do not erase another person's right. The Verse of the Throne places every practical duty beneath God's life, knowledge, and rule. The final verses return the whole chapter to faith and prayer. In this way, the sūrah carries a society from its creed to its contracts and then brings it back before its Lord.

The Prophet gave this long chapter a place in ordinary homes. Abū Hurayrah reports his instruction, *"Do not turn your houses into graves"*, followed by the reason that the deceiver does not enter a house where Sūrah al-Baqarah is recited (Muslim). Abū Umāmah reports another instruction to recite it because taking hold of it is a blessing and abandoning it is a cause of regret (Muslim). These reports do not turn recitation into sound without obedience. They place revelation where people sleep, trade, disagree, raise children, and make decisions. The protection promised to a house belongs with a chapter that reforms what happens inside houses and beyond them. Its opening letters first teach restraint before hidden meaning; its next verses teach certainty, reverence, and action. The commentary therefore begins where the sūrah begins, with three recited letters that are fully preserved even though their final meaning has not been disclosed.

---

## Verse 2:1

> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm

**THREE NAMES BEFORE THE FIRST SENTENCE**

The chapter opens with ***“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”***. Each part is the name of an Arabic letter, said on its own. The three do not join to make a normal word. Twenty-nine sūrahs open with such letters, though the sets are not all the same. The same three stand at the head of another chapter: (3:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”**). A longer set opens a third: (7:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd”**). These links show that the form is planned, not a stray mark left on the page. Since the letters are part of the revealed text, they are read in prayer even when their last sense is not known. This is why the opening first asks for care, not guesswork. Before the Book tells us what to think or do, it makes us voice what God sent in the form He sent it. The point is plain: true reading starts by taking the text as it is, not by changing it into what we wish it had said.

**WHERE A FIRM CLAIM MUST STOP**

A strong early view leaves the last sense of these openings with God. Al-Shaʿbī took this path, and the same care is linked to Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and Ibn Masʿūd. This did not make the letters blank. Because God does not speak in play, they have a wise end even if that end has not been made plain to us. The early stance joins faith with a curb on false claims. A person may read the words with trust while refusing to invent a gloss. This fits the praise of those firm in knowledge. When they reach what lies past their grasp, they say, (3:7 — **“We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord.”**). Reason is at work here, since it knows the line between proof and a hunch. It follows that we should not say the letters mean nothing. We should say that no sound report from the Prophet has fixed one full gloss for them, so our firm claim must stop where firm proof stops.

**EARLY VIEWS HELD AT THEIR TRUE WEIGHT**

Other views were kept, and each offers food for thought. Ibn ʿAbbās is linked to a reading in which alif points to Allah, lām to Gabriel, and mīm to Muhammad. On that view, three signs trace the path of the Book: God sends it, Gabriel bears it, and the Prophet receives it. Another report reads them as divine gifts, grace, and rule. A third gives the sense *I am Allah; I know*. Some early scholars took the set as an oath or as a name for the sūrah. These views do not have equal proof, and none should be put into the text as its sole meaning. The reason for citing them is more modest: they show why early Muslims did not hear mere noise in the opening. They also show why one neat claim must not shut out all else. The Book is still clear Arabic, (12:2 — **“Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand”**). In other words, a clear Book can bear a sign whose full aim its Lord has kept from us.

**COMMON LETTERS AND SPEECH NO ONE CAN MATCH**

The place of these letters also makes a case about the Book. The first Arabs knew each sound and spoke with the same set of letters. The Qur'an came (26:195 — **“in a clear Arabic tongue”**), not in a code they could not hear. Yet this sūrah soon calls on each doubter to meet a test: (2:23 — **“And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it”**). The letters put the raw means of speech on the hearer's tongue before that call is made. Therefore, knowing the parts is not the same as making the whole. A pile of stone may lie in plain sight, but it does not raise itself into a sound house. In the same way, full use of the script gave the first hearers no power to match the Qur'an. What follows is a clear challenge, not a hunt for dates or codes in the value of each letter. The effect is to turn what is common—the alphabet—into a sign of the unmatched Book made from it.

**HOW TO READ WHEN AN ANSWER IS WITHHELD**

The first verse teaches a skill needed in all that comes next. Al-Baqarah will give laws, past events, moral tests, and signs in the world. Some points will be plain at once; some will yield more with time. A reader who makes up an answer for each gap will bend both kinds. A reader who rejects all that he cannot explain will fare no better. ***“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”*** sets a wiser course: keep the words, test each claim, name the early views with care, and leave the rest with God. That is why this brief verse still speaks in our own time. We can post a bold answer in seconds, while sound proof may take years to gain. The verse gives no praise to a sure tone with no ground. Nor does it bless lazy doubt. Its demand is exact speech and, where proof runs out, a calm stop. The same set opens Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt, (29:1 — **“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm”**), just before the next verse asks, (29:2 — **“Do people think once they say, “We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test”**). Here it stands before a book of guidance. In both places, we begin as people who receive before we claim the right to explain.

---

## Verse 2:2

> This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE ANSWER PLACED AFTER THE PRAYER**

The first full statement points to what is already being recited: ***“This is the Book!”*** The form can point to something near while giving it the rank of something set high. It may also look back to the part of the Qur'an already sent down, or to the Book promised before this moment. Each reading serves one fact: the words now heard are not a loose page or a private thought, but the known Book from God. The link with al-Fātiḥah sharpens the point. The worshipper has just asked, (1:6 — **“Guide us along the Straight Path”**), and the answer is placed at the start of this chapter. Guidance will not be made from desire alone; it will come through this Book. This is why the raised way of pointing does not put the Book out of reach. It gives weight to the gift now within reach. What stood in God's knowledge and promise has come close enough to be read, learned, and obeyed.

**A CLAIM ABOUT THE BOOK, NOT ABOUT EVERY REACTION**

The next words state, ***“There is no doubt about it”***. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and a large group of the early teachers read this as doubt about its source: it has come from God. Another early reading hears a command within the statement—do not doubt it—but the plain claim comes first. The sentence does not pretend that no human being will raise an objection. This same sūrah soon speaks to people who are in doubt and gives them a test. The difference is between doubt found in a hearer and fault found in the Book. A clouded eye does not place a stain on the object it fails to see. Therefore, denial cannot cancel what the sentence asserts about the text itself. Another chapter joins the claim to its ground: (32:2 — **“The revelation of this Book is—beyond doubt—from the Lord of all worlds”**). Its truth, source, and message give no sound cause for doubt, even when a person supplies doubt of his own.

**ONE LIGHT WITH TWO VERY DIFFERENT EFFECTS**

The verse then names the Book as ***“a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. At first, that may sound too narrow, since the lost need guidance most. The distinction is between the presence of guidance and the benefit drawn from it. The Book sets out the road for humanity, so its light is not locked away. Yet only a willing heart follows that road and receives the fuller gift of being helped along it. The same rain can meet open soil and sealed stone without becoming two kinds of rain. In the same way, the Book remains guidance while people meet it in opposite states. The Qur'an says of the believers, (41:44 — **“˹O Prophet,˺ “It is a guide and a healing to the believers. As for those who disbelieve,”**), then speaks of deafness and blindness in those who turn away. The reason for naming the mindful is therefore not that others have no access to the words. It is that the guarded heart lets the words do their guiding work.

**MINDFULNESS AS A SHIELD MADE OF DEEDS**

Mindfulness here is not a mood that comes and goes. Ibn ʿAbbās described the people meant as those who keep away from joining partners with God and act in obedience to God. The early image given to ʿUmar by Ubayy bin Ka'b makes the point vivid. When asked about this guarded state, Ubayy asked how a man walks through a path thick with thorns. ʿUmar replied that he gathers his clothes and takes great care. Ubayy said that this is the state in question. The image joins fear to action: the traveller sees what can tear him, draws his life in, and chooses each step. Since such care is already active, revelation gives it sight and direction rather than leaving it as bare fear. It can also grow, which means that the verse does not divide people into a fixed class of the worthy and everyone else. The Book trains the care by which it is received. Rank before God rests on that quality: (49:13 — **“Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you.”**).

**THE ROAD SHOWN AND THE HEART ENABLED TO WALK**

The word guidance bears two related acts that must not be confused. One is to show truth, mark the false road, and call a person toward the right one. A human caller and a Book guide in this sense: (42:52 — **“And you are truly leading ˹all˺ to the Straight Path—”**). The other act is to place faith, resolve, and success within the heart. That act belongs to God, as the limit on human power makes plain: (28:56 — **“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best”**). The two acts explain the force of the whole verse. The Book is present, clear, and free of doubt; no one is barred from its call. Still, mere contact with a text does not force trust into a resistant will. Those who guard themselves receive both a road they can see and help to travel it. Thus the answer to the prayer in al-Fātiḥah is neither a map without divine aid nor aid without a revealed map. It is the Book as guidance, received by a heart prepared to follow.

---

## Verse 2:3

> who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them

**FAITH MOVING FROM THE HEART INTO THE WORLD**

The people guided by the Book are first described as those ***“who believe in the unseen, establish prayer”***. The two acts belong together. Faith starts with trust in truths that the eye cannot inspect, but it does not remain a hidden claim. It gives the body a fixed act and the day a fixed order. Prayer then keeps the unseen near through words and movements performed in the seen world. This is why the verse moves from inward assent to public worship without placing a wall between creed and deed. A claim lodged only in the mind has not yet shaped a life, while a movement with no faith behind it is only a shell. A later verse gives the fuller pattern: true faith names Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets, then describes those (2:177 — **“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans”**) and who establish prayer. The order is not a list of unrelated virtues. It shows one trust taking form in worship and care.

**WHAT LIES OUTSIDE THE REACH OF THE SENSES**

The unseen includes what is hidden from ordinary sight and cannot be known by the senses alone. Ibn ʿAbbās named Paradise, Hell, the Bridge, the Scale, resurrection, and the reckoning; other early readings included what comes from God in revelation. God, the angels, the final hour, and realities of the next life are not placed in one class because they are all hidden in the same way. Some are beyond sense by their nature, while some are future events whose time or form is withheld. What joins them is that sound news from God, not direct sight, is the ground for faith in them. Therefore, belief in the unseen is not permission to believe every strange tale. The source of the report matters. Faith accepts what God and His messengers disclose, and it refuses to turn lack of sight into proof that nothing exists beyond sight. The moral force appears in (67:12 — **“Indeed, those in awe of their Lord without seeing Him will have forgiveness and a mighty reward”**). Conduct changes before the hidden becomes visible, which is why such trust can test the heart.

**PRAYER THAT IS KEPT STANDING**

To establish prayer is more than to perform a few outward motions. The early explanations include its set times, cleansing, standing, bowing, prostration, duties, and due limits. They also include the inward life that makes those acts worship: attention, humility, and remembrance. The wording therefore presents prayer as something built and kept upright. If one support is dropped on purpose, the structure is no longer being cared for as the verse describes. This does not demand a feeling of equal strength at every prayer. It demands that prayer be given its appointed form and that the heart be called back whenever it wanders. The command to Moses joins its purpose to its form: (20:14 — **“and establish prayer for My remembrance”**). Another verse gives prayer a moral effect, since (29:45 — **“˹genuine˺ prayer should deter ˹one˺ from indecency and wickedness”**). The point is not that every person who goes through the motions will at once cease to sin. It is that prayer kept upright trains remembrance that resists sin, while careless prayer is being deprived of its intended force.

**PROVISION RECEIVED, THEN ALLOWED TO FLOW**

The final trait turns toward other people: ***“and donate from what We have provided for them”***. The sentence first names the giver of the provision and only then the act of spending. Wealth is in a person's hand, but its source is God's gift; this is why giving is not the owner's boast over the one who receives. The word “from” also matters in the English line. The duty is drawn from what has been given, not from what a person does not possess, and it does not command the loss of every means of support. The early readings include the required alms as well as wider gifts in obedience to God. They also keep the field broad enough for family support, relief of need, and willing charity. Since the provision came as a trust, holding it has a moral limit. Another verse makes that relation clear by commanding people to (57:7 — **“donate from what He has entrusted you with”**). Thus the verse closes its movement from hidden faith to embodied prayer and then to wealth released for good. What God gives reaches the heart as truth, orders the body as worship, and passes through the hand as mercy.

---

## Verse 2:4

> and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter

**THE REVELATION NOW PLACED IN THE MESSENGER'S CARE**

The description continues: ***“and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺”***. What has come down to him is the Qur'an. Faith receives both its source and its claim to rule life. The wording says “revealed,” which means that the Messenger is neither its author nor the owner of its truth. He receives, conveys, teaches, and lives by what comes from above. This is why love for a messenger cannot be separated from trust in the message he bears. It is also why praise for the Qur'an without submission to it falls short of the faith named here. The Book repeats the command even to people already called believers: (4:136 — **“O believers! Have faith in Allah, His Messenger, the Book He has revealed to His Messenger, and the Scriptures He revealed before.”**). Faith therefore has to be renewed through assent and obedience. A revelation may be in a person's home, memory, or language while its judgment is still kept outside his choices.

**A PRESENT BOOK THAT HONOURS REVELATION BEFORE IT**

The sentence widens the line of faith to include ***“and what was revealed before you”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explained that believers accept what the former messengers brought from their Lord, without denying one messenger while claiming another. This joins the Qur'an to one history of divine speech. The Torah, the Gospel, and the other books were true as God sent them. Faith in the final Book does not require contempt for their divine origin. At the same time, this verse does not place every later copy, claim, or law on one level with the Qur'an. The final revelation confirms the truth sent before it and judges what people now attribute to it. That relation is stated with care: (3:3 — **“He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth, confirming what came before it”**) and the final Book stands as (5:48 — **“a supreme authority on them. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed”**). Therefore, continuity does not erase the final Book's authority, and final authority does not erase the honour due to earlier revelation.

**ONE PORTRAIT, WITH A SPECIAL PLACE FOR LATER BELIEVERS**

An early reading linked this verse in a special way to people of earlier Scripture who then accepted the Qur'an, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those with him. On that reading, the prior verse describes believers from the Arabs, while this one honours people who held to a former revelation and then received the last. The distinction has a clear point: such people did not have to betray Moses or Jesus in order to follow Muhammad; true loyalty to the former message led them to the later one. Yet the wording also gives a single portrait of every mindful believer. Faith in all revelation is required of the whole community, not only converts from Judaism or Christianity. The wider reading is stronger as the basic rule because another command addresses all believers with both books. The special reading then identifies a clear example within that rule. The Qur'an teaches the shared confession in direct form: (29:46 — **“We believe in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to you. Our God”**). The one God is the reason true messages cannot be enemies.

**CERTAINTY ABOUT THE LIFE THAT COMES LAST**

The portrait closes with the words ***“and have sure faith in the Hereafter”***. The Hereafter is the life that comes after this near one, and the early explanations unfold it into resurrection, standing before God, reckoning, the scale, Paradise, and the Fire. Certainty gathers these truths into more than a vague hope that life may continue. It treats return and judgment as fixed facts. This is why certainty about the end gives weight to every earlier trait. Revelation matters because its claims will be tested; prayer matters because a servant will stand before God; giving matters because wealth and its use will be judged. A person can repeat the word “afterlife” while living as if no account will come, but that is not the sure faith praised here. The opposite voice admits that it has only a guess: (45:32 — **“We think it is no more than speculation, and we are not convinced ˹that it will ever come˺.’””**). Sure faith closes that gap between speech and expectation. In other words, certainty about the unseen is measured by the weight it gives to present conduct before the future becomes seen.

---

## Verse 2:5

> It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful

**THE VERDICT THAT GATHERS EVERY PRIOR TRAIT**

After three verses of description, the passage gives its judgment: ***“It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord”***. “They” gathers everyone marked by the traits just named: trust in the unseen, prayer kept upright, wealth shared, faith in the Qur'an and earlier revelation, and certainty about the final life. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd also applied the verdict across both groups discussed by the early readers—believers from the Arabs and believers from the People of the Book. The point is that origin does not create two ranks of guidance when the same faith and obedience are present. Nor can one trait be detached from the rest and made a claim to the whole verdict. The reason is that guidance orders the whole person. Prayer without faith, giving without submission, or belief in an earlier messenger joined to denial of the last does not match the portrait. This is why the final judgment comes only after the full set. Guidance has produced a joined life, not a badge carried by ancestry or group name.

**GUIDANCE AS A FIRM PLACE GIVEN BY THE LORD**

The people are not praised as self-made seekers who found the road by skill alone. Their guidance comes from their Lord, the One who creates, owns, sustains, and brings them step by step to maturity. The early explanations describe their state as light, clear proof, mercy, and insight from God. Because its source is the Lord, guidance is both a truth shown and help granted to follow it. The verse also gives the sense of being set firmly on guidance rather than touching it for a moment. A passing burst of feeling is not the same as a settled direction that bears the weight of choices. Another verse describes the inner side of that gift: (39:22 — **“those whose hearts Allah has opened to Islam, so they are enlightened by their Lord”**). The opened heart and the revealed road meet. In other words, the source of the gift does not cancel the duty carried by its receiver. Therefore, the believer neither credits himself as the maker of guidance nor treats himself as a passive object with no duty. The gift enables the walk, and the traits in verses 3–4 show the walking.

**THE REPEATED SUBJECT THAT CLOSES EVERY RIVAL CLAIM**

The clause repeats its subject—***“and it is they”***—before completing the verdict with ***“who will be successful”***. The repetition places weight on these people and on the path that formed them. It rules out the thought that lasting success can be secured by rejecting the Book while seeking its promised end. Yet success here is larger than one pleasant outcome or a short period of ease. Ibn ʿAbbās described it from both sides: reaching what was sought and escaping what was feared. The positive end is God's pleasure and Paradise; the rescue is from wrath and the Fire. The Qur'an defines the final measure in the same two-sided way: (3:185 — **“Whoever is spared from the Fire and is admitted into Paradise will ˹indeed˺ triumph”**). This is why a gain that ends at death cannot be the full success of a verse shaped by certainty in the Hereafter. True success must survive the judgment that follows death.

**A SUCCESS WHOSE FIRST FRUIT APPEARS BEFORE THE END**

Although its complete form belongs to the next life, success begins to shape this one. Guidance frees a person from worshipping appetite, public praise, wealth, or inherited error. Prayer gives the day an axis, charity loosens the grip of possession, and certainty about return gives present choices a true scale. None of this means that the guided life is spared grief, loss, or struggle. This is why hardship cannot by itself decide whether a life has failed. The Qur'an opens another portrait with (23:1 — **“Successful indeed are the believers”**) and at once points to (23:2 — **“those who humble themselves in prayer”**). It also says, (91:9 — **“Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul”**). Therefore, success is not merely a prize attached at the end to an unrelated life. Its signs are already present in faith, humble worship, moral cleansing, and open-handed use of God's gifts. Verse 5 closes the opening portrait by joining the road to its end: guidance from the Lord is the beginning, and success with Him is the arrival.

---

## Verse 2:6

> As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe

**WHEN REFUSAL HARDENS INTO A DESCRIPTION**

The passage now turns from those who accept guidance to ***“As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them”***. The translation adds the sense of persistence because the verse describes refusal that has settled into a trait. This difference matters because the words do not close the door on every person who is now outside the faith. Many who first fought the Messenger later believed. The early reports point instead to people whose refusal had become firm. Some readers named hostile chiefs in Makkah. Some named learned men among the People of the Book who knew the signs yet hid them. Others took the words as a broad account of all whom God knew would die in denial. Ibn ʿAbbās linked the verse to people who rejected what came from the Lord while claiming faith in earlier books. The Arabic term for this denial comes from a root for covering or hiding. Arabs used the same root for night because its dark veil covers things. They also used it for a sower who covers seed with soil. This background matters because denial here covers a truth already made known. This is not a passing doubt or an honest search that has not yet reached its end. It is a stance held against the light already given. That is why a like verdict says, (10:96 — **“Indeed, those against whom Allah’s decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe—”**). God speaks with full knowledge of their end. No human being may turn that knowledge into a guess about another person’s heart.

**WHAT A WARNING PLACES BEFORE ITS HEARER**

The middle of the verse sets two acts side by side. In this case, the result for the hearers is the same. Yet warning means more than the bare transfer of facts. The early teachers defined it as news joined to fear. The reason is that it names a danger while time remains to avoid it. A prophet warns out of care, not from a wish to harm or shame. The warning is like a clear sign placed before a road that ends in ruin. If a driver passes the sign, its truth and worth do not vanish. The equality here concerns the response of these fixed rejecters. Therefore, it does not make faithful warning equal to silence in the Messenger’s duty. He is still told, (88:21 — **“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind”**). At the same time, force lies outside that duty: (88:22 — **“You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺”**). Another verse draws the same line: (5:99 — **“The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you reveal and what you conceal”**). A rejected warning still makes the truth plain and fulfils a trust. The point is that refusal cannot turn sound delivery into failure. Nor can anyone use this verse to give up on a person after one refusal. No preacher knows that person’s final state. The message is therefore given with care, while its fruit is left to God.

**A LIMIT SET ON GRIEF, NOT ON THE MESSAGE**

The close, ***“or not—they will never believe”***, allows both a present and a future sense. They do not believe, and they will not believe. The same words return in another place: (36:10 — **“It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe”**). Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the Messenger longed for all people to believe and follow the right road. This is why he did not carry the task of opening every heart. It did not tell him to stop speaking. The Qur’an keeps a person’s answer and God’s gift of guidance in the same view. The truth is offered in the open: (18:29 — **“And say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord. Whoever wills let them believe,”**). Yet the Messenger cannot make faith take root in one he loves, (28:56 — **“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best”**). God does not wait for events to learn what people will choose. In other words, His prior knowledge is complete before the choice appears in time. Their choice is also real, the warning is just, and the answer remains theirs. The verse thus sets a bound on grief without making unbelief small. It also prepares for the next verse, where sealed hearts and covered sight show the end of long refusal. Each act of hiding truth trains the soul to hide it again. A warning should be met while the heart can still hear it, not tested until refusal has become its settled name.

---

## Verse 2:7

> Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment

**A SEAL FORMED AFTER LONG REFUSAL**

The judgment now moves from a fixed refusal to the faculties that refusal has spoiled. After ***“Allah has sealed their hearts”***, a closed document or vessel supplies the image: nothing enters, and nothing within is changed. The heart in Qur’anic speech is not merely the place of emotion. It is where a person understands, weighs, trusts, and chooses. This is why another passage speaks of people travelling so that (22:46 — **“their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen”**). A sealed heart is therefore a mind and will that no longer receive truth as truth. The early readings do not treat this state as an innocent lack of information. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Qatādah linked the seal to refusal of what had been made clear. The Qur’an states the cause elsewhere: (4:155 — **“is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few—”**). The order matters because it guards divine justice from a false charge. God does not punish willing faith by making faith impossible. Persistent denial is judged by the loss of the very openness that denial kept abusing. In other words, the seal is God’s act, while the guilt that meets that judgment belongs to those who chose rejection. The verse before this one named their settled stance; this verse shows the fitting end of that stance within them.

Mujāhid pictured the process with an open hand. With each sin, one finger closes until the hand is shut; then the closing is stamped. Abū Hurayrah also reports that the Prophet described a dark mark appearing on the heart when a servant sins. Repentance and a plea for pardon polish it, while repeated sin makes the mark grow until it covers the heart (al-Tirmidhī). The Qur’an gives the same moral sequence: (83:14 — **“But no! In fact, their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit”**). This evidence explains why the seal must not become an excuse for despair after one wrong act. A stain may be cleaned, and the report expressly places repentance before the final covering. The danger lies in protecting the stain, repeating its cause, and training the conscience to call darkness light. Because each refusal makes the next one easier, punishment can begin before the final punishment: the person loses the unease that once called him back. A good deed may open the way to another good deed, while an evil deed may invite another evil deed. That pattern does not remove choice. It shows how choices form the chooser. The seal is the dreadful point at which a long habit of turning away has become a settled inability to welcome what was repeatedly refused.

**THREE FACULTIES AND ONE COMPLETE LOSS**

The sentence continues with ***“and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment”***. Hearing is joined to the heart under the seal, while sight receives the separate image of a covering. Sound may reach an ear from every side, and meaning may reach a heart through many paths, so a seal pictures the shutting of the whole faculty. Sight faces what lies before it, so a veil pictures the barrier. These are not claims that the people cannot hear ordinary speech or see ordinary objects. They hear recitation without yielding to it and see signs without reading them as signs. A parallel verse joins all three: (16:108 — **“They are the ones whose hearts, ears, and eyes are sealed by Allah, and it is they who are ˹truly˺ heedless”**). Another describes listeners whose inward veil leaves them unable to grasp the Qur’an, (6:25 — **“but We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears. Even if they”**). The difference between physical use and moral benefit is therefore central. Eyes can work while insight is blind, and ears can carry sound while obedience remains deaf. By contrast, God sends calm into believing hearts (48:4 — **“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers”**), showing that the same inward place can receive a gift when it receives guidance.

The scale of the final punishment matches a loss that has reached every gate by which guidance is received. The heart does not understand, the hearing does not profit, and the sight does not take warning. Yet the verse is not permission to declare living people sealed by private judgment. Revelation disclosed the fate of the people addressed; ordinary believers do not know another person’s end. Its present warning is turned first toward the self. A lie defended today, a duty mocked tomorrow, and a truth repeatedly pushed aside can alter what the heart is able to love. This is why the movement from stain to seal matters. The warning urges repentance while remorse still speaks. It urges careful listening before sacred words become mere sound. It also urges sight that reads created things as signs rather than scenery. The punishment named at the end belongs to the Hereafter, but its road begins when moral awareness is willingly dulled. The opposite road also begins now: truth is admitted, pardon is sought, and each faculty is returned to the purpose for which God gave it.

---

## Verse 2:8

> And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers

**A NEW GROUP ENTERS THE ACCOUNT**

After sincere believers and open rejecters, the words ***“And there are some”*** introduce a third public condition. These people stand among the community and speak its language, yet their inward allegiance runs elsewhere. Ibn ʿAbbās applied the first setting to hypocrites among the Aws and Khazraj and to others who followed their conduct. This condition took public form in Madinah, where Islam had gained enough strength for false profession to offer safety or influence. Makkah had shown the reverse pressure: some believers were forced to hide faith while enemies held power. The difference is moral and must not be blurred. Concealed faith under force protects truth within; concealed disbelief uses a false claim of faith for gain. The verse therefore does not condemn caution under persecution. It exposes the use of sacred speech as a mask. Later revelation describes people who swear that they belong with the believers although (9:56 — **“they are not. They only say so out of fear”**). Their presence explains why the surah gives more space to hypocrisy than to open disbelief. A known enemy can be faced as an enemy. A false friend can enter trust, shape counsel, spread doubt, and retreat behind words that sound faithful. The reason is that a spoken claim may win access before conduct reveals the hidden aim.

**THE TWO GREAT TRUTHS PLACED ON THEIR TONGUES**

Their claim begins with ***“who say, “We believe in Allah”***. It then reaches the end of human accountability through ***“and the Last Day,””***. These are not small or vague articles. Faith in Allah governs the source, purpose, and worship of life. Faith in the Last Day governs its reckoning and final result. Together they stretch from the unseen Lord to the day when every hidden thing is shown. Yet the verse reports these truths as speech rather than settled conviction. This is why a correct sentence can still be a lie when the speaker uses it to present a heart he does not possess. Another passage records a fuller claim: (63:1 — **“When the hypocrites come to you ˹O Prophet˺, they say, “We bear witness that you are certainly the Messenger of Allah”—and”**), then adds that God bears witness to their lying. The Messenger truly is God’s messenger; the lie lies in their claim to bear sincere witness. In the same way, the two beliefs named here remain wholly true. What fails is the bond between the tongue and the heart. The verse does not lower the worth of confession. It shows why confession has its proper life only when inward assent and outward loyalty meet.

**THE DIVINE VERDICT BEHIND THE PUBLIC CLAIM**

The decisive answer is ***“yet they are not ˹true˺ believers”***. Human observers hear the profession; God knows the hidden denial. The verdict also reveals what the opening reference had gathered: this is a recognisable class, not one unnamed speaker. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, and al-Suddī read the line as a disclosure meant to keep believers from being deceived by appearance. Ibn Jurayj described the hypocrite through broken agreement: deeds oppose publicity, hidden aims oppose speech, and conduct in absence opposes conduct in company. The Qur’an later exposes the same split through action. When such people rise for prayer, (4:142 — **“they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all”**). Their mouths can say what their hearts deny, as another verse states directly: (3:167 — **“that day—for saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. Allah is All-Knowing of what they hide”**). The ruling concerns hypocrisy in creed, where an outward claim conceals inward rejection. It must not be carelessly applied to every believer whose actions are weak. Sinful conduct may carry a trait of hypocrisy without proving that faith is absent from the heart. The verse gives a grave category, not a weapon for reckless accusation.

**DISCLOSURE WITHOUT A CULTURE OF SUSPICION**

God’s exposure of the hidden group protects the community, but it does not grant ordinary people access to unseen hearts. Clear lies, betrayal, and patterns of harm can be judged by sound evidence. Private suspicion cannot become proof. This balance follows from the way revelation itself deals with the matter: God discloses what people could not know unaided, while believers remain bound to justice in what they can know. The hypocrites themselves fear a surah that will expose their inward state, (9:64 — **“The hypocrites fear that a sûrah should be revealed about them, exposing what is in their hearts. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Keep mocking!”**). Their concealment finally fails because the One they name in speech already knows what they hide. It will fail again when they swear before Him as they once swore before people, (58:18 — **“On the Day Allah resurrects them all, they will ˹falsely˺ swear to Him as they swear to you,”**). The verse thus turns inward as well as outward. It asks whether worship, hope, fear, and preparation for return agree with the creed spoken aloud. A sound profession should be guarded, but it should also be made truthful through loyalty and deeds. The cure for hypocrisy is not silence about faith. It is a heart that means what the tongue says and a life that does not secretly work against its own confession.

---

## Verse 2:9

> They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it

**A PLOT THAT CAN NEVER REACH GOD**

The claim in the last verse is now shown as a plan. ***“They seek to deceive Allah”*** does not say that the plan can work. A lie works among people when one person sees an act but does not know the aim behind it. God sees both the act and the aim. Ibn ʿAbbās says these people denied God in secret while they dared to think that they had fooled Him. Al-Ḥasan linked the words to their effort to fool God’s Messenger. This link is sound because the Messenger brought God’s call, and their show of faith was meant to evade the rule that met open foes. They wished to keep the shield of the Muslim group while they hid their war against its faith. It is like a man who puts on a mask in full light but stands before One who saw him make it. The mask may mislead those near him for a time. It cannot veil him from God. Even vast schemes lie bare before their Lord: (14:46 — **“They devised every plot, which was fully known to Allah, but their plotting was not enough to ˹even˺ overpower mountains”**). The force of the charge lies here. They place fraud within a bond with the One from whom no thought can hide. Thus, the first name in the verse makes the whole plan absurd before its harm is traced.

**THE BREACH OF TRUST AMONG BELIEVERS**

The full turn comes in ***“and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it”***. Ibn ʿAbbās names Abū Bakr and the Companions as the first believers whom they tried to fool. The false claim of faith gave them a way into a group held by trust. It could let them hear plans, shape talk, gain aid, and pass word to foes. This is why hypocrisy can harm a group in ways that an open foe cannot. Yet this verse is not leave to search hearts or charge each weak Muslim with secret denial. God has told us what He knew of this group. We know no such thing on our own. People may judge a clear lie, a breach of trust, or a known act of harm. They must not turn doubt into proof. Faith does not ask for blind trust, but it does bind judgment to what can be shown.

A later verse sets their scheme beside their prayer: (4:142 — **“Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them. When they stand up for prayer,”**). It then says that they pray to be seen. The act is real, but its aim is false. This matters now because a person may still use good words or good deeds to build an image. The first use of the verse is not to brand someone else. It is to ask whom one seeks to please. A weak act done for God is not the same as a planned show done for praise. Nor does one bad thought prove lack of faith. But a heart should fear the habit of making worship serve the gaze of people. This self-watch guards pure intent and keeps the warning from feeding harsh claims about others.

**THE SNARE CLOSES ON ITS MAKER**

The plot points out, but its deepest wound turns back. They may gain a short span of safety or rank. Yet no gain can make their hidden denial safe before God. Ibn ʿAbbās says that they did not know God would tell His Prophet what lay hid in them. Their lie could thus lead to shame in this life, while its full due waits in the next. It also harms them before they are exposed. One lie calls for the next. Each new role adds fear that the mask will slip. The liar must spend more thought on the tale and less on the truth. Soon the role that was meant to serve him starts to rule him. His first false gain thus plants the seed of a far greater loss.

The same law is stated for evil plots as a whole: (35:43 — **“behaving arrogantly in the land and plotting evil. But evil plotting only backfires on those who plot. Are they awaiting anything”**). This does not claim that no scheme can hurt an innocent person. It says that the plotter cannot keep its evil from his own account. A trap may catch its marked prey, yet still close on the hand that set it. Nor does a short win decide the end. Past foes made plans, (13:42 — **“but Allah has the ultimate plan. He knows what every soul commits. And the disbelievers will soon know”**). Their fault was not shrewd thought as such. Good plans join true means to a good end. Their fault was the use of lies against God’s cause, joined to the mad hope that the Lord of the end could be left out of the count. Once God’s knowledge, the scarred soul, and the Last Day are put back into view, the claimed gain is loss.

**WHEN CLEVERNESS MAKES A PERSON BLIND**

Their failure to perceive is the last part of the fraud. They watch other people with care, yet fail to see what they do to their own souls. This is a sharp form of blindness. A person can read each face in a room, spot each risk, and still miss the plain fact that God sees him. He may call that skill, though it has cut him off from the truth he most needs. The verse therefore draws a line between craft and sound sense. Craft asks whether other people believed the lie. Sound sense asks what the liar has become through it. Because the first question fills their sight, the second fades. The question a person keeps asking will shape both his next act and his inner life.

The cure begins with plain truth before God. It asks that speech, prayer, and loyal deeds agree. It also asks for swift return when a hidden aim is found. The longer a lie is fed, the more facts must be bent to keep it alive. But no bent tale can outrun the record. When people plot against God’s signs, they are warned: (10:21 — **“˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah is swifter in devising ˹punishment˺. Surely Our messenger-angels record whatever you devise.””**). Today, in daily life, truth may seem costly at once, while fraud may seem cheap. This verse counts the costs that the fraud leaves out: loss of a clean heart, fear of being known, harm to those who gave trust, and judgment before God. The faithful path may give up a quick edge, but it keeps the self whole. Deceit, by contrast, first cheats the one who chose it.

---

## Verse 2:10

> There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies

**THE HEART CAN FALL ILL WHILE THE BODY IS SOUND**

The fraud of the last verse has an inward cause: ***“There is sickness in their hearts”***. The heart here is the seat of trust, will, and moral sight. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, and Qatādah all linked this sickness to doubt and hypocrisy. Ibn Zayd was plain that this is an illness in faith, not a bodily disease. That guard is vital. The verse does not shame a sick body, nor does it let people brand those who face mental distress as hypocrites. A person may bear great pain and still have a heart full of faith. The sickness named here is chosen falsehood that has begun to spoil how truth is received. Doubt by itself is not always blameworthy; an honest doubt can seek light and yield when proof comes. This doubt hides behind a claim of faith, feeds on envy, and refuses the truth it fears will cost too much. The Qur’an links the same inward flaw to a fear that God and His Messenger might be unjust: (24:50 — **“Is there a sickness in their hearts? Or are they in doubt? Or do they fear”**). Such fear shows that the heart no longer sees its Lord or His rule as it should. The image of illness fits because sin has harmed a power meant for sound use. The heart still acts, but it no longer judges in a sound way.

**HOW A CHOSEN ILLNESS IS MADE TO GROW**

The next words join judgment to what they brought first: ***“and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment”***. The order bars the thought that God first forced a sound heart into hypocrisy and then blamed it. Sickness is already there. They feed it through lies, and God lets its reach grow as a just result. The same order is made clear when a people first turn away and then meet a matching judgment: (61:5 — **“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. For Allah does not guide the rebellious people”**). Their first turn is real, and God’s rule over what follows is also real. This is why each fresh sign can lead two hearts in two ways. Those who welcome the truth gain faith: (9:124 — **“it has increased them in faith and they rejoice”**). Those who mock it gain more of the filth they chose: (9:125 — **“But as for those with sickness in their hearts, it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness,”**). The light did not change; the response did. A cure can save one patient who takes it, while its refusal leaves another illness room to spread. Yet this verse goes beyond a mere natural result. God rules that result, withholds aid from proud refusal, and makes the new state fit the old choice. By contrast, He gives more help to those who take the first steps of trust: (47:17 — **“As for those who are ˹rightly˺ guided, He increases them in guidance and blesses them with righteousness”**).

**WHY THE LIE STANDS BESIDE THE PAIN**

The verse closes by naming the cause: ***“for their lies”***. The nearest lie is their claim in verse 8 that they believed in God and the Last Day. Those truths were sound, but they used them to paint a false picture of their hearts. This makes lying more than one fault in a long list. It is the tool by which their inward breach enters public life. One accepted recitation points to their habit of telling lies, while another points to their denial and their charge that God’s message was false. The two senses meet in their case. They deny truth within and speak a false claim without. A later surah sets the same pattern before the reader. The hypocrites give true words about the Messenger, yet God states that their claimed witness is a lie because the words do not report what they hold within: (63:1 — **“surely Allah knows that you are His Messenger—but Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars”**). The painful end therefore suits the deed. Their tongues were used to dull warning, gain safety, and cause pain through fraud. They would not let the truth of the Last Day rule life, though they spoke its name. Now the Last Day gives the lie its due. This does not make every lie equal to hidden disbelief, but it shows why lying is not small. Each lie trains the heart to split speech from fact. When that split is nursed in faith itself, it becomes the sickness this verse lays bare.

**THE IMAGE OF SICKNESS ALSO POINTS TOWARD A CURE**

A grave diagnosis need not make a living reader lose hope. The same Qur’an that shows sick hearts also comes as their cure. Its call is addressed to all people as (10:57 — **“a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts,”**). Cure begins when the lie stops. A person admits the hidden fault to God, asks for pardon, restores what the lie harmed, and lets true words lead to true acts. He also keeps watch over early signs: joy when truth is harmed, anger when it corrects him, the wish to look good rather than become good, and ease in saying what his heart does not own. These signs are not grounds to despair or to pass a final verdict on oneself. They are grounds to seek help before a habit grows. Today, the warning reaches public faith, private prayer, work, family, and every place where a trusted word can be used as a mask.

The contrast in this verse also teaches how to approach revelation. The Qur’an is not bare data placed before a cold mind. It tests love, pride, fear, and will. It is (17:82 — **“a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss”**). Healing comes as the reader yields to truth and acts on it; loss grows as the reader uses each sign as fresh ground for scorn. Thus the heart is not healed by learning how to speak about faith while guarding its old disease. It is healed by letting God’s word expose, cleanse, and guide. The warning remains severe because untreated hypocrisy grows. The hope remains real because the door to honest return is open while life remains.

---

## Verse 2:11

> When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”

**A WARNING MEETS A CLAIM OF GOOD INTENT**

The next scene gives the hidden group a chance to hear plain advice: ***“When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!””*** The one who speaks is not named, so the stress falls on the truth of the warning and their set reply. They are not left with no word from outside their own circle. Someone names the harm, yet they turn the charge on its head. Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and from Ibn Masʿūd identify the corruption here as disbelief and acts of revolt against God. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and Qatādah also link ruin in the land to disobeying God or urging others to do so. In this setting, the harm includes a false show of faith, aid given to foes, and efforts to bar people from the path. These deeds break trust and pull the group in two ways at once. The words extend the view across the land. Sin is not sealed inside one heart when it shapes speech, ties, and public acts. It moves through the lives of other people. This is why a command found elsewhere joins the state of the land to God’s prior gift of order: (7:56 — **“Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope”**). What God has set right must not be torn apart under a fair name.

**CORRUPTION IS KNOWN BY MORE THAN ITS LABEL**

The verse shows how moral words can be seized and turned. The people do not say that some harm is needed to gain a larger good. They deny the class of harm and claim the class of repair for themselves. Their wording makes the boast closed and strong: all we do is set things right. Yet a good name cannot cleanse a bad deed. Real reform must face facts about its means and fruit. It serves truth rather than hiding it. It keeps trust rather than using trust as a path to betrayal. It draws people toward what God made sound rather than blocking that road. A sign painted with the word peace cannot turn a road toward harm into a safe road.

The Qur’an does praise true work for peace. Secret talk, which can host plots, becomes good when it urges charity, right conduct, or peace between people: (4:114 — **“There is no good in most of their secret talks—except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people.”**). When two groups of believers fight, the command is first to make peace, but the peace must also stop wrong and uphold what is fair: (49:9 — **“then make peace between both ˹groups˺ in all fairness and act justly. Surely Allah loves those who uphold justice”**). These tests keep peace from becoming a soft word for leaving wrong in place. They also keep zeal for truth from becoming a plea for needless strife. Reform seeks a just peace by sound means. The hypocrites fail both sides: their hidden ties feed harm, and their public claim shields it from cure.

**WHY SELF-DECEIT MAKES CORRECTION HARD**

The warning begins with an act of speech because harm can still be named and stopped. Their answer shows why that opening may close. A person who knows an act is wrong may yet feel shame, seek pardon, and change. A person who crowns the same act as reform has built a wall around it. Advice then sounds like an attack on goodness. The next verse will state that they fail to sense what they do, but the seed is seen here: their moral map has been reversed. They count a split heart as wise care, a lie as safe policy, and aid to falsehood as public good. Because the label soothes them, the result no longer warns them or drives them to change.

This does not mean that good intent has no worth. It means that a claim of good intent cannot be the last judge of an act. A person may aim at peace and still choose a means that breeds fear, lies, or wrong. He must be willing to learn from the fruit and test the means by God’s rule. The chiefs whom Ṣāliḥ warned were described as those (26:152 — **“who spread corruption throughout the land, never setting things right.””**). Their power and speech did not earn them the name they might have liked. In the same way, a Muslim should be more ready to ask whether a plan sets things right than to insist on being called a reformer. The humble heart can bear that test. The sick heart needs the good title too much to let the deed be seen.

**A TEST FOR EVERY PUBLIC PROMISE OF REFORM**

The verse gives a lasting rule without giving readers leave to hurl its charge at each rival. Today, leaders, groups, firms, families, and lone users of a screen can all wrap a harmful choice in words such as peace, care, safety, or reform. The right response is not to distrust every such word. It is to ask for truth, just means, and sound fruit. A policy that rests on lies does not become good through a kind name. A truce that hands the weak back to an oppressor is not the fair peace urged by revelation. A harsh act is not made wise merely because its maker says that order was the aim. At the same time, a hard but just step should not be called corruption only because it causes strain. Names must follow moral facts, not replace them.

The first use of this test is near the self. When sound advice arrives, one should pause before defending a cherished aim. The adviser may be wrong, but the claim must be weighed rather than brushed aside. True reform can bear clear proof, admit loss, and change course. It joins good ends to lawful means and seeks God’s pleasure rather than the praise due to a saviour. The broad charge to Qārūn holds the two sides together: (28:77 — **“And be good ˹to others˺ as Allah has been good to you. Do not seek to spread corruption in the land,”**). Good is done, harm is refused, and both are judged before God. The hypocrites keep the name of the first while they do the second. The verse trains the believer to refuse that split in private plans as much as in public life.

---

## Verse 2:12

> Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it

**GOD OVERTURNS THE NAME THEY GAVE THEMSELVES**

The reply is brief, firm, and framed to wake the hearer: ***“Indeed, it is they”***. The speakers in the last verse had shut the debate by claiming that all their efforts were to set things right. God now rejects both the claim and the scale by which they made it. The opening calls for close notice, while the pointed pronoun sends the charge back to its true owners. The believers who warn them are not the source of the ruin. The people who hide denial, break trust, and aid falsehood are. Their view of themselves cannot change God’s verdict. This matters because a good title is one of the first shields a bad course seeks. If the actor can fix the name, he hopes to silence all thought about the deed. Revelation tears away that shield. Good and evil are not made equal by a crowd’s praise, a leader’s claim, or a fine aim stated after the fact. The same rule appears in a broad command: (5:100 — **“Good and evil are not equal, though you may be dazzled by the abundance of evil.”**). Moral fact stands even when the eye is drawn elsewhere. The words here restore that fact before they explain why the guilty group misses it.

**THE CORRUPTORS ARE KNOWN BY WHAT THEIR COURSE BREAKS**

The verdict names those ***“who are the corruptors”***. Disbelief and revolt against God are the acts identified by Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and Qatādah add the harm of urging such revolt. Ibn ʿAbbās also reads their work as a hindrance: leaders lead followers away while the followers fail to grasp where they are being led. These strands show why the charge is not about a lone fault with no reach beyond the sinner. The group joins false faith to acts that block the path, disclose the believers’ affairs to foes, and loosen the bonds of truth. Their course makes harm spread. Each new follower can give the false path one more voice and a wider field.

The Qur’an can use corruption for clear loss in both life and land. A later figure speaks well in public, then goes out to (2:205 — **“strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle.”**). Another passage states, (30:41 — **“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done,”**), so that some results may be tasted and people may return. Here the first wreckage is faith and trust, but it does not stay unseen. A false ally can twist plans, make truth seem weak, and draw others into the same split. Those who mislead bear more than their own load: (16:25 — **“as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear”**). This is why hidden denial may become public corruption even before streets or fields show its mark. It breaks the moral roots from which just life grows.

**A FAILURE TO SENSE WHAT THEIR OWN DEEDS HAVE BECOME**

The final clause, ***“but they fail to perceive it”***, returns to the blind spot named in verse 9. Their lack of sense does not make the harm unreal or free them from blame. They have been warned. They refuse the warning because their false account feels safer than the truth. At first, a person may know that he is using a fair name to mask a wrong deed. With time, the name can dull his sense of the wrong. Praise from friends, gain from the plan, and anger at each critic then look like proof that he is right. The heart no longer uses pain caused, trust broken, or truth barred as signs to stop. This is why self-praise is so grave here.

One early reading draws a further line within the group: the followers do not sense that their chiefs lead them astray. This does not erase the followers’ duty, but it explains how ruin can pass through ranks. The chief calls harm reform; the close circle repeats the claim; and those farther out inherit both the name and the deed. Each layer makes the next less likely to see. The Qur’an warns of efforts that are lost while their makers still think they do good: (18:104 — **“˹They are˺ those whose efforts are in vain in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good!””**). Mere force of intent is therefore not a safe guide. A sound conscience needs truth from God, honest counsel from others, and the will to review results without first protecting pride.

**JUDGING HARM WITHOUT CLAIMING KNOWLEDGE OF HEARTS**

This verse gives a sure ruling about the people God exposes. It does not give each reader a free right to name every rival a corrupter. That misuse would copy the same pride the verse rebukes. God warns, (53:32 — **“So do not ˹falsely˺ elevate yourselves. He knows best who is ˹truly˺ righteous”**). Today, acts and their known results can be judged by revealed and just standards. Hidden creeds and final ends belong to God. The line lets a community oppose lies and harm without turning suspicion into knowledge of hearts. The verse is strongest when it trains the self before it arms the tongue. A person should ask what trusted bond his plan keeps, what truth it serves, whom it may lead, and whether he can still hear sound blame. Those checks do not make moral judgment weak. They keep it clean. Past peoples lacked enough people who would bar such ruin: (11:116 — **“If only there had been among the ˹destroyed˺ peoples before you, ˹O believers,˺ virtuous individuals who forbade corruption in the land”**). So faithful life needs clear warning as well as humble self-review. The hypocrites fail at both points: they spread harm, then strip the warning of its power by calling themselves healers. The believer seeks the reverse. He names harm by God’s scale, welcomes proof even when it cuts pride, repairs what he has broken, and never treats a fine name as proof of a sound deed.

---

## Verse 2:13

> And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know

**FAITH IS SET BEFORE THEM AS A LIVED REALITY**

A second appeal now follows the ban on ruin: ***“And when they are told, “Believe”***. The call is not for one more public claim, since they already say that they believe. It asks for the truth that joins heart, tongue, and deed. The next words, ***“as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe”***, point to faith already lived in front of them. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas identify these people as the Prophet’s Companions. Ibn ʿAbbās also names Ibn Salām and those with him, who believed from among the People of the Book. They trusted God, His Messenger, His books, the life to come, and the commands that put faith into practice. The comparison does not turn truth into a vote or ask for blind praise of a crowd. It points to those who received the message with a whole response, in contrast to those who borrowed its words as a mask. The close of this surah shows the same shared faith: (2:285 — **“and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books,”**). Their cure is thus not better acting. It is the faith whose outward form they had copied while refusing its core.

**PRIDE CALLS COSTLY FAITH FOOLISH**

Their scorn breaks out in the words ***“as the fools believe?””*** They mean the Companions who left homes, bore the anger of foes, shared wealth, and put loyalty to God above quick safety. The hidden group reads those costs through a small measure of gain. To risk rank for truth looks foolish if rank is the highest good. To give up wealth for a brother looks foolish if the self has the first and last claim. To obey when desire pulls elsewhere looks foolish if freedom has been cut down to doing what desire wants. Their slur therefore reveals their scale more than it describes the believers. They count what faith gives up at once, but they never count what its truth gains.

The lives they mock give a different account of wisdom. The people of Madinah welcomed those who came to them and (59:9 — **“give ˹the emigrants˺ preference over themselves even though they may be in need.”**). That choice may look like loss in a short account, but God calls those saved from greed the ones who thrive. The hypocrite guards the near gain and spends the lasting self; the believer may spend a near gain and guard the lasting self. This is the heart of the clash. It is not that faith praises poor thought or asks people to ignore cause and effect. It widens the field of cause and effect to include duty, the state of the soul, death, and judgment. Once those facts are counted, the sacrifice that seemed foolish may prove to be the sanest choice.

**THE CHARGE IS RETURNED BY PERFECT KNOWLEDGE**

The answer begins, ***“Indeed, it is they”***, and ends with those ***“who are fools, but they do not know”***. In this setting, folly is failure to know one’s true good and the path that secures it. These people are skilled at reading the balance of power and shaping speech for each group. But skill at gaining a short edge is not wisdom when the edge leads to ruin. A sailor may know each rope on the ship yet be a fool if he steers straight toward the reef. In the same way, social skill without a true end can make error more swift, not less. Their plan saves an image for a day and spends the soul that must face God.

The Qur’an often parts showy skill from sound knowledge. Some past peoples took pride in what they knew when clear proofs came, then were (40:83 — **“˹ultimately˺ overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule”**). The hypocrites themselves can look and sound strong: (63:4 — **“When you see them, their appearance impresses you. And when they speak, you listen to their ˹impressive˺ speech.”**). Neither fine speech nor worldly sense repairs the broken aim within. The end of knowledge is lost when pride first decides what may count as true. God’s reply is exact because He knows both the hidden end they seek and the end they cannot see. Their insult cannot lower the people of faith, but it does disclose the pride that blocks their own return.

**A DIVINE VERDICT IS NOT A LICENSE TO MOCK**

God names the folly of a known group whose hearts He has exposed. A believer must not copy their habit by treating every person of less skill, schooling, wealth, or rank as beneath notice. The later rule is plain: (49:11 — **“Do not let some ˹men˺ ridicule others, they may be better than them, nor let ˹some˺ women ridicule other women,”**). Human rank is often wrong because it sees one gift, one fault, or one day. God sees the whole person. That limit guards justice. The verse also does not condemn careful questions. The Companions did ask, learn, weigh reports, and seek clear guidance. What it condemns is pride that decides in advance that humble trust must be beneath the proud.

This danger remains close today. A person may call prayer naïve, restraint weak, charity wasteful, or repentance a loss of face. He may also use the verse in reverse and call sound study foolish merely because it tests an inherited claim. Both moves avoid the hard work of truth. Faith does not fear sound proof, and reason does not reach its proper end by leaving God out. The test is whether knowledge bows when truth becomes clear and whether it guides the self toward its real good. The hypocrites fail because they make their own status the measure of wisdom. The faithful learn from those who bore the truth with honesty, seek proof without scorn, and count the Last Day among the most real facts in any choice.

---

## Verse 2:14

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”

**ONE CLAIM IS MADE IN THE OPEN MEETING**

The passage now lets us hear both sides of the double life. ***“When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.””*** Ibn ʿAbbās places Abū Bakr and the Companions among those met in the first setting. The hypocrites do not merely keep quiet or speak with common care. They claim the same deep and true faith as the people before them. Their words seek safety, trust, and a share in any good that comes to the Muslim group. This scene adds detail to the broad claim of verse 8. There the tongue spoke; here the audience and aim come into view. The claim changes with the company because it was made to manage the company. A later passage shows the same split: (3:119 — **“When they meet you they say, “We believe.” But when alone, they bite their fingertips in rage.”**). The meeting did not make them faithful, and the time apart did not make them cease to be so. The two scenes uncover one fixed heart using two forms of speech. Like a coin stamped with a new face each time it changes hands, their words take the mark most likely to pass in the group before them. The gain may be near, but each use makes true trust harder to restore.

**THEIR EVIL ASSOCIATES ARE HUMAN GUIDES INTO WRONG**

The scene turns with ***“But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you”***. The source wording calls these associates their devils. Early readers such as Ibn ʿAbbās understood the first setting to include chiefs, soothsayers, and leaders in evil. The translation brings out their role rather than limiting the line to unseen beings. The Qur’an itself speaks of (6:112 — **“enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception.”**). A devil in this human sense is not a person one merely dislikes. It is one hardened in revolt who adorns falsehood, calls others to it, and uses rank to keep them near. This matters because their lead is moral and chosen, not a spell that erases the follower’s will.

The act of going back to these guides also shows where the hypocrites feel bound to give a true report. With believers they offer a claim. With their chiefs they offer assurance of firm loyalty. The private room strips the public words of their worth. This does not make every difference between public and private speech a sign of hypocrisy. Good sense may choose a mild word, keep a trust, or wait for the right time to speak. The fault here is a clash in allegiance: faith is claimed to one group while aid and approval are pledged to those who oppose it. Another passage shows (5:52 — **“those with sickness in their hearts racing for their guardianship”**) because they fear a turn of fate, then facing regret for what they hid. Fear of losing access can make a person serve both rooms, but it cannot make the two loyalties true at once.

**MOCKERY IS THE EXCUSE THAT EXPOSES THE PLOT**

They close their report with ***“we were only mocking.””*** Ibn Isḥāq transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation that their claim of faith was meant to fool and deride the believers. Mockery here is not a harmless laugh shared by friends. It treats the believers’ faith as a prop and their trust as proof that they can be played. It also lets the speakers boast before their chiefs. By calling the public claim a joke, they assure the private group that no real bond was formed outside it. Their humour is thus an act of rank: the mockers place themselves above people whose trust they use. The laugh also binds the hidden group, since shared scorn can serve as a harsh pledge that none of them will cross sides.

The Qur’an closes the easy shelter of such an excuse elsewhere. When people hid behind the same excuse, they were asked, (9:65 — **““We were only talking idly and joking around.” Say, “Was it Allah, His revelations, and His Messenger that you ridiculed?””**). The next answer is stark: (9:66 — **“Make no excuses! You have lost faith after your belief. If We pardon a group of you, We will punish others”**). Not every failed joke has this weight. The object, aim, and state of the speaker matter. In this verse, the mockery is joined to hidden denial and a planned false claim. It is the final word in a scheme, not a stray word followed by regret. What they call play therefore reveals the grave truth of what they chose.

**A DIVIDED TONGUE FORMS A DIVIDED LIFE**

The warning reaches beyond one meeting in Madinah. Today, people move through home, work, places of worship, private chats, and public screens. Some change of tone is normal and wise. A child, a close friend, and a large group need not be addressed in one style. The danger begins when the core claim itself changes for gain: loyalty before one side, contempt before the other, and no speech ruled by truth. Each audience then owns a piece of the speaker. Fear grows because one room may hear what was said in the next. Faith seeks a sounder form of life. Private words need not reveal every secret, but they must not betray the truth claimed in public. A believer may fail, fear people, or speak poorly without becoming one of the hypocrites named by God. The verse gives no right to read hidden creed from one uneven act. It does give a clear test for the self: one should note whether, when no faithful friend is present, one mocks what one praised in their company. The cure is to choose one Lord and one moral bond across all rooms. That wholeness may cost a false ally, a passing gain, or the thrill of a cruel joke. It frees the tongue from serving each new crowd and keeps the heart from being split by the masks it has to defend.

---

## Verse 2:15

> Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance

**THE MOCKERY RETURNS AS A JUST REPLY**

The boast at the end of verse 14 receives an answer from above: ***“Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance”***. The translation makes the return clear. God does not share the petty need that drove their scorn, nor is His act a lie or a cruel joke. Their mockery comes back as shame and just loss. Early readers explain the form as a fitting reply whose name matches the sin: they mock the faithful, so their own plan is exposed and made a cause of scorn. Some also held the wording as a divine act affirmed as revelation states it, while denying every flaw found in human mockery. Both lines guard the same truth. God is not fooled, unjust, or in need of sport. He gives their deed its due. A like answer appears when hypocrites mock small gifts: (9:79 — **“for giving only the little they can afford. Allah will throw their mockery back at them,”**). The return fits because the proud stance is itself overturned. Those who thought they watched from above become the ones displayed, while the faith they mocked proves sound.

**THE LAST DAY MAKES THE REVERSAL VISIBLE**

Ibn ʿAbbās links this reply to the Hereafter, when a hope of entry is shown and then closed before them. The Qur’an gives a grave scene of that loss. Hypocrite men and women ask the believers to wait so that they can take from their light. The answer tells them to go back and seek light; then (57:13 — **“a ˹separating˺ wall with a gate will be erected between them. On the near side will be grace”**). Their old claim of being with the believers returns as a plea: (57:14 — **“The tormented will cry out to those graced, “Were we not with you?” They will reply, “Yes ˹you were˺.”**). They had shared streets, meetings, and the outward acts of the group, but they had not sought the light at its source in true faith.
