Ibn Jurayj transmits the shape of the shouting across the street: one party said, you killed him, and the other answered, no, you killed him. The same account stands with the Successor Abd al-Rahman b. Zayd, whose gloss divides the crowd exactly into accusers and accused. The point is that no third posture existed in the scene. Since the killer moved among them by night and planted the body at a stranger's door, the population woke into a dispute with exactly two sides and no evidence, and the verb the Book chose for them keeps the memory of how each side pushed.

**WHAT WAS CONCEALED AND WHAT BROKE IT OPEN**

The verse closes on the intervention that ends the quarrel: ***“but Allah revealed what you concealed”***. The concealment has three layers in the narrations, and the disclosure broke all three at once. The murderer hid the deed itself, moving the corpse in the dark; his partisans hid the truth beneath their accusations; and the wider public hid whatever it knew behind the comfort of an unsolved case. Mujāhid takes the closing phrase as simply what you were hiding, and the gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās presses it against the crime with full force: *"demonstrating what you hid with regard to his murder"*. The disclosure then arrives not as testimony but as an event. The struck corpse lived, named the hand that had killed him, and died again, and the two sides of the street fell silent before a witness neither side could cross-examine. In other words, the revelation that broke the concealment was a resurrection borrowed for a day, which means the trial of the murder was folded inside a demonstration of the returning life. The command that will follow in the next clause is therefore the hinge between a criminal case and a creed, since the instrument of justice is also the proof of the afterlife.

**THE DEVICE NOBODY WAS ASKED TO EXPLAIN**

A standing puzzle hangs over the instrument of the disclosure, and the tradition answers it with the right measure of restraint. The question of the revived corpse, and of the cow's flesh as the instrument of reviving him, receives no catalogue of rationales; what the narrative supplies instead is a boundary for the asking. The law does not oblige the servant to discover the rationale behind each divine act, and the One whose wisdom encompasses the act needs no one's permission to choose its form. The Book itself marks the device as demonstration in the plainest terms — (2:73 — **“Allah brings the dead to life”**) — and the demonstration is doing double work: closing a murder case for one audience and holding up a mirror to the afterlife for every audience. The present-day reader will find that this sequence calibrates the questions worth asking about the acts of God. Enquiry about reported events may run to their meaning and their moral economy; it stops at the threshold of the chooser's wisdom, because the stopping is itself a discipline the story of this murder teaches more sharply than most.

---

## Verse 2:73

> So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand

**A STRIKE WITH A PART OF WHAT WAS SACRIFICED**

The instruction is one sentence long and it ends the case: ***“So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs”***. The pronoun of the strike returns to the slain man, carried on the masculine sense of the person rather than the feminine form of the soul-word, and the scene gathers three dead things at once: a dead man, a dead limb, and an animal already slaughtered. The transmission of Mujāhid fixes the moment in one line of narrative: *"he struck him with the cow's thigh and he rose alive and said that so-and-so had killed him, then he returned to his death"*. Another account has the blow fall from the tongue or the tail of the animal, and the revived man naming a killer or two among his own cousins before he died again. The differences between these reports are held without strain, because none of them touches what the verse itself makes plain: the instrument of the case was the flesh of the sacrifice, and the demonstration was a return to life granted for a day.

**THE PART NOBODY WAS TOLD TO KEEP**

The specifying instinct that ran through the hunt now reappears among the interpreters themselves, and the tradition handles it with an instructive discipline. The scholars differed over which organ was used: one naming the tongue, since the tongue is the instrument of speech and the dead man was about to speak; another the base of the tail, since the human frame is said to be assembled there; others the thigh, or a bone from her bones. Against all of them stands the certain minimum — an organ from her organs — and the narrated epistemic rule is the sharpest thing in the material. Any part of the cow would have produced the miracle, so the unspecified part carries no benefit in religion or in life; had it carried benefit, the Book would have named it; the matter was left vague because it was delivered vague, and the learned response is to leave it exactly so. The lesson reaches far past this episode, since the reader who demands the withheld details of every reported sign is demanding what the report deliberately declines to give.

**THE LAWYERS TAKE UP THE DEAD MAN'S WORDS**

The revived man's sentence — my blood is with so-and-so, so-and-so killed me — entered the legal tradition as an argument, and the argument divided the schools. In the transmissions of Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, the great early jurist Malik cited the slain man's words as proof for the validity of the collective oath procedure in homicide, the fifty-oath mechanism by which a victim's kin press a murder claim when direct proof is missing. The rejection came from al-Shafi and the majority of the scholars, who held their own position correct and refused the probative analogy; (2:178 — **“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man,”**) marks how tightly the standing law of murder is drawn, and a miracle-bound declaration sits outside its ordinary evidence. The difference between the two sides turns on exactly that boundary. In this story the dying declaration was certified by a device no courtroom can reproduce — a corpse revived by the flesh of a divinely commanded sacrifice — which means it stands as a miracle's testimony and not as a template for witnesses. What follows for the legal mind is therefore a caution in both directions: the event may illuminate the moral gravity with which the dying man's words were treated, and it may not be pressed into a rule of proof the standing law never drew from it.

**ONE SOUL REVIVED, EVERY SOUL PROMISED**

The closing clause does the work of a creed: ***“so that you may understand”***. The understand here is glossed from one direction as believing in the resurrection after death, and from another as the reasoning that follows from a single example: the One capable of reviving one soul is capable of reviving every soul, and the reader is asked to pass from the witnessed case to the promised one. The chapter builds this argument with visible architecture, returning to the life-after-death demonstration more than once — the raising after the first death, the thousands who fell and rose, the traveller who passed a town in ruins and watched its people stand again, and the patriarch who asked to be shown how the dead are given life and was answered with four birds (2:260 — **“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?””**). Each return presses the same point from a different angle: what happened before can happen again, and the precedent is meant to carry the reason forward. The modern reader who accepts the logic of precedent in every other field will find the chapter asking only that the logic be applied without a special exemption for death.

---

## Verse 2:74

> Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE HEARTS THE SIGNS COULD NOT WET**

The address of you in this verse has drawn a real dispute, and both candidate referents are in the earliest glosses. Ibn ʿAbbās takes the hearts as the hearts of the slain man's heirs, and the narrative gives that reading its force: when their kinsman rose and named them, they answered with a denial made in full knowledge. Al-Awfi transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās the scene in these terms: *"when he was asked who had killed him, he said that his nephews had killed him; then he died again, and they denied the truth while they knew it"*. The other reading, standing with Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, and the body of interpreters, takes the address to the Children of Israel entire — the community whose character the whole section has been prosecuting. A second axis of the same question then appears in the reading of the audience as such: the rebuke can stand against those who stood at the incident and watched a corpse testify, and it can stand against the later contemporaries who heard the account recited and turned from what it teaches. The difference between the two referents is smaller than it looks, since a group's settled culture is exactly what produces a family's denial at the crucial hour, and the layered reading lets the verse address the event and the inheritance of the event at once. What turns on the pronoun is therefore the scope of the warning, not its substance: whether the charge names the heirs who lied or the nation whose habit made the lie easy, the diagnosed condition is the same hardening after the clearest sign.

**WHAT HARDNESS MEANS AND WHY STONE IS THE MEASURE**

The hardening itself is named with a verb whose root family carries dryness and the withered state, and the glosses gather its senses like wounds on one body. The heart is described as dried and withered, which is the going of mercy and softness from it; another sense has it grown coarse; a third has it blackened. The comparison then does the diagnosis's work: ***“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock”***, ***“or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers”***. The likeness is to the stone in its hardness and its barrenness toward the effect of deeds, and the strange word at the head of the sentence marks how far the state stands from expectation — the hardening arrives after the very event whose whole purpose was to remove it. The particle joining the second clause reads either as a plain and or as the sharper nay, and both keep the escalation: like stone, or past stone. The choice of stone over the harder metals is itself instructive, because the stone still keeps the possibility of what the heart has lost. Iron is harder and it is not the measure; the stone is, since the stone in this very passage does three things the hardened heart refuses to do.

**THREE KINDS OF STONE, THREE DEGREES OF ALIVE**

The catalogue of stones is graded with a careful hand. The first produce gushing rivers — the image at the top of the scale, a rock giving drink to beasts and men, the very figure of a life-bearing heart; the second ***“others split, spilling water”***, giving less but still giving; the third ***“while others are humbled in awe of Allah.”***. The water in the image is the water the Book everywhere treats as life and the means of life — sent down from the sky, rising from beneath the ground, and figured inside the creation of living things themselves — so that the rock which gushes is a dead thing producing what the living need, and the contrast with the heart that produces nothing is total. The falling of the third kind is then the summit of the scale rather than its floor, since a thing that fears is a thing still addressed by its Lord. The Book presses that consciousness onto the most solid objects it can name: (59:21 — **“Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have certainly seen it humbled”**) — and the mountain of Moses furnishes the historical picture of the same truth, where the appointed sight levelled the peak to the ground before the man who asked to see (7:143 — **“If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me.” When his Lord appeared to the mountain,”**). The point is that the entire created order is awake to its Author; it is the human heart alone in this passage that sleeps.

**WHEN EVEN STONE REMEMBERS ITS LORD**

The tradition about living stones is not confined to this passage, and its reports draw the picture from every side. The Prophet's own words about the greeting stone — *"I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me before I was made a prophet, and I know it even now"* — are transmitted in Muslim; the mountain that answered affection — *"This is a mountain that loves us, and we love it"* — stands in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections; and the palm-stump that wept beside the pulpit, answered with the Prophet's embrace and his words *"It weeps for the remembrance it used to hear"*, is transmitted by Tirmidhī and Nasāʾī. A further reading of the three kinds of stone takes them as three kinds of human weepers — those who weep much, those who weep little, and those whose weeping stays in the heart and never reaches the face — and the psychology of the comparison is exact. Even the mountain's surrender is drawn into the argument, since the whole of creation is described as hymning its Author in voices the audience cannot hear — (17:44 — **“that does not glorify His praises—but you ˹simply˺ cannot comprehend their glorification. He is indeed Most Forbearing, All-Forgiving”**) — and some of the early readings hold that all three kinds of stone in the verse act out of fear of God, the gushing and the splitting included. In other words, the catalogue is not really mineralogy. It is a hierarchy of responsiveness laid against a congregation, and the stones occupy every rank above the one the hearts have chosen.

The verse closes the comparison by turning from the metaphor to the account: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. The closing phrase is glossed from two directions by the same authority. Ibn ʿAbbās takes it as the assurance that God will not leave the transgressions unpunished, and he also reports the sense that the what you do includes what is hidden, the denials spoken in the heart while the tongue answers the questioner. The transmitted variant shifts the closing verb itself, moving from you do to they do as the accusation widens from the immediate audience to everyone who behaves like it. Against the certainty of the accounting stands the patience of the interval, since the same clause has been read as respite — God is not heedless, and He gives time until the appointed term. The two readings balance without cancelling: the unawareness is excluded, the haste is not implied. For congregations that hear the passage in every generation the application is exact and unsentimental. These days the pattern of hardening is not a story about a single family or a single town; it is the standing risk of anyone who watches a sign arrive and files it away unopened, and the closing clause is the reminder that filing is also doing.

---

## Verse 2:75

> Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it

**A HOPE THE HISTORY CANNOT CARRY**

The verse that follows the catalogue of signs turns, for once, on the people who received them best: ***“Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you”***. The opening interrogative is one of rejection, and the tradition unpacks its force as a single instruction: do not be so eager, for their record is already written. The expression of longing at the head of the sentence is stronger than hope. The tongue of the language marks it as the soul's strong attachment to attaining its object, arising from the intensity of desire and the force of the will — and that is precisely the disease being diagnosed in the address, a longing for the belief of a people whose book of signs has already closed, which means the desire is spent on a door that history has shut. The address itself is disputed in the best way. The received views run from the Prophet and the believers together, to the believers alone, to the Ansar in particular, whose alliance and neighbourhood with the Jewish tribes had made them eager for their conversion; the transmitted view from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil takes the line as directed to the Prophet alone, carrying the comfort of do not grieve at their belying you. The difference between the readings softens the edge rather than dulling it, since every candidate for the address shares one posture: standing at the end of a long persuasion and still hoping it might work.

**WHO THE GROUP IS THAT HEARD AND ALTERED**

The reason the hope is being sent home is then given in one clause of history: ***“though a group of them would hear the word of Allah”***, ***“then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it”***. The identity of the group is settled in two directions across the glosses, and both deserve keeping. Mujāhid, Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddī take the group as the scholars of the community in its later generations — the class who heard the revelation recited and then altered what it carried. The transmitted view from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil places the group at the mountain, as the seventy men chosen by Moses for the appointment of his Lord, and the distortion charged to them is precise: they returned to their people declaring that their Lord had promised forgiveness where the commandments could not be borne, a softening of the law pronounced in the very presence of its descent. The narrated examples of the later alteration run to two items above all: the description of the awaited prophet, which was rewritten, and the penalty that had stood in the text and was taken out. The word they were heard hearing is the Torah itself, recited to them by Moses, and the hearing is not metaphorical — the tradition has them listening to the recitation as the verses arrived.

The crime in the clause is layered past translation, and every layer matters. The distortion is reported as reaching the words themselves, or the sense standing behind them, or both at once, and the two verbs of the clause frame it as a deliberate act of the learned. The report of Qatādah keeps the whole sequence in one line: *"they are the ones who used to hear the words of God and then alter them after they had understood and grasped them"*. The double qualification attaching to that act is the moral centre of the verse. The corruption came after understanding, so that error is ruled out; and it came knowingly, so that the excuse of haste is ruled out too. What turns on those two words is the whole difference between a mistake and a crime, since the alteration of a text one has understood is a decision made against one's own knowledge. The Book traces the same behaviour to its root in the covenant's own ledger — (5:13 — **“But for breaking their covenant We condemned them and hardened their hearts. They distorted the words of the Scripture”**) — and the hardened hearts of the preceding verse and the distorted words of this one are therefore the same condition seen from inside and outside.

**THE CONTEMPORARIES AND THE RECKONING OF COMPANY**

The verse's logic then reaches past its first audience, and the narrated context makes the reach practical. The believers had taken great pains over the conversion of their neighbours, and the counsel here is not coldness toward a people but realism about a pattern. The contemporaries of the Prophet may not have stood at the mountain or rewritten the pages, and the tradition still counts them into the account on one principle: a generation that does not abhor the misdeeds of its forefathers is counted among their company. The standard applied is neither inheritance nor ancestry but approval, and by that standard the party addressed in the verse is anyone who keeps the silence that makes alteration safe. The two identifications of the group converge exactly here, because the scholars who alter and the publics that consent are one machinery; the first supplies the distortion and the second supplies the market for it. The reader today who has watched a text handled carelessly by those paid to guard it will find the verse's expectation-management reading as current advice: persuasion has a duty, and it also has a horizon set by the honesty of its audience, because neither half of the equation belongs to the persuader alone.

The immediate demonstration of the diagnosis arrives in the following movement of the passage, where the private and public faces of the group separate — (2:76 — **“When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺,”**). The pattern there is the pattern named here in embryo: speech arranged by audience, knowledge treated as a bargaining chip rather than a trust. The closing words of the present verse — after understanding it, knowingly — thus stand as the verdict that the next scene will illustrate, and the illustration is drawn from ordinary conversation rather than from any miracle. What follows for those who read the passage as a manual of trust is exact. Knowledge of revelation carries two custodial duties at once: it may not be altered, and it may not be withheld for advantage, and the verse indicts the group on both counts in a single sentence.

---

## Verse 2:76

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”

**TWO AUDIENCES, TWO SPEECHES**

The exposure runs on one contrast and the verse never lets it soften: ***“When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.””***. The public sentence is a claim of belief, and the glosses unpack what the claim meant in the mouths that used it: an acknowledgement that Muhammad is a prophet, and the one their own book gave good tidings of — with, in some readings, the small print that he was a prophet but not a prophet for them. The private scene then opens with the leaders of the group speaking to its weaker members, and the mechanics of the hypocrisy are laid out in the glosses with the precision of a case file. The men in question were converts who had found the community's growing strength in Madinah a good investment; their disclosures of the good tidings were the tokens of a purchased sincerity; and the rebuke that greets them in private is not disbelief but a question of strategy. The attribution of the speech to the whole group follows the tongue of the language once more — some utter it and the rest hold their silence, and the whole is named for the part it permits. What the juxtaposition teaches is the shape of the disease itself, because the same mouth that sells a creed by the verse keeps the verse priced for the next bargain.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THEY TRIED TO PRICE**

The disclosure in question is identified in the glosses with a consistency that matters: ***“But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you”***. What had been made known to them was the description of the awaited prophet standing in their own book — the passage the leaders now wish had stayed behind their teeth. The wider sense of the disclosure-language carries three degrees in the earlier readings: what God has commanded you, what God has decided for you, and the knowledge He has given you or eased into your hands. The identification is consistent because the whole scene turns on a document both sides can quote. Another reading takes the reference to the prophecies themselves, so that the private question becomes: whether an open affirmation of his prophethood hands him a proof to take out against them at the reckoning. The particle governing the purpose of the disclosure is itself disputed, and the dispute is worth one line: the same letters read as intent — so that they may argue with you — and as consequence — with the result that they argue with you. The question as it was spoken runs ***“so that they may use it against you before your Lord?”***, and the location clause at its end draws the same width of reading. It has been taken as the courtroom of the last day, where the two parties will be questioned face to face; as a plain concerning, the argument standing about your Lord; and, in a usage the language supports, as in the sight of your Lord, the phrase that often stands equivalent to in the book of your Lord.

**THE ARGUMENT THEY WERE GUARDING**

The economics of the secrecy are then stated by the scene's oldest account, and the account runs through named transmitters. The converts turned hypocrites used to tell the believing Arabs about the punishments their forefathers had suffered, and the community's reprimand fell on them in these terms: *"Do you tell them what God has opened against you, so that they say: we are nobler before God than you?"* — Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddi transmit the report, and the fear inside it is the fear of an argument lost. A second account gives the same transaction its doctrinal value: the verses of the good tidings were exactly the ammunition the believers needed to end the debate, which means every disclosure shortened the road of the argument and every concealment lengthened it. The reason the leaders reprove the disclosure rather than the faith of the men who made it is strategic rather than pious, since the market they are protecting is the market in evidence. The parallel surfaces of the same behaviour are already marked elsewhere in the revelation, where the same public sentence hides the opposite private one — (2:14 — **““We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.””**) — and where the private face is not mocking but rage.

**THE KEEPERS AND THE PROOF TAKEN OUT AGAINST THEM**

The verse ends inside the leaders' own speech, on a question that indicts the intelligence of the conspiracy: ***“Do you not understand?””***. The gloss takes the charge precisely as a rebuke of foresight: the speakers are told they have no sense of the fact that these very men will contend with them at the reckoning, holding what they were told against them. The irony the question carries is the verse's last weapon. The men pricing their knowledge are told, by their own side, that the price is a proof taken out against its keepers, and the day of the mutual questioning turns the hoarded passage into testimony for the other party. The companion exposure of secret behaviour keeps the moral in view at the level of the heart rather than the marketplace — (3:119 — **“˹O Prophet,˺ “˹May you˺ die of your rage!” Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart”**) — and the next verse of the present passage will close exactly there, on the God who knows the concealed and the shown. For communities that trade in religious knowledge today the passage is a standing audit of motive. Disclosure that serves the truth is a duty; the same disclosure withheld to keep an opponent ignorant is the exact commerce this verse prices, because its ledgers close at a door no strategy has ever locked.

---

## Verse 2:77

> Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal

**A BACK ROOM THAT IS NOT A BLIND SPOT**

The verse asks a question the previous scene has already answered. The leaders of the city had met in private and asked each other whether the believers should be told what was revealed to them, lest they argue with the leaders before their Lord. The reply does not debate the strategy. It names the room's missing wall: ***“Do they not know”***, ***“that Allah is aware of what they conceal”***. The question is not a question. The grammar of the negative interrogative here is the grammar of an affirmation, and the glosses press it: they know, and the knowing is the point. The particle that introduces the clause is the particle of supplement, so the sentence joins this concealment to every other one. The range of the knowing is stated as wide on purpose. The tradition hears the clause as covering this matter and all other matters, so that the men are told plainly why the back room cannot hold. Ibn ʿAbbās fixes the two parties of the scene in a single line. The hidden talk is talk kept among themselves, and the proclaimed talk is talk aimed at the prophet and his companions.

**HIDDEN IN COUNSEL, PROCLAIMED IN PUBLIC**

The second half of the sentence completes the map: ***“and what they reveal”***. The pair of nouns is the verse's whole anatomy of the case. What the leaders hid was the recognition: the testimony sitting in their own books about the awaited prophet, and the reading of the signs they recognized in the man from Mecca. What they proclaimed was the market version: the claims of inheritance, the counted days, the standing of beloved sons. The secret talk recorded in the scene before this one was itself a piece of legal strategy. If the believers learn the texts, they will argue with us from our own shelves, so keep the shelves shut. The answer of the verse is that the shelves were never shut. The hearing that recorded the counsel is the hearing that will read the trial, and the two directions of speech — the whisper of the chamber and the statement of the market — are entered in the same record. The parallel in the final revelation draws the same portrait in one line: (9:78 — **“Do they not know that Allah ˹fully˺ knows their ˹evil˺ thoughts and secret talks, and”**). The arithmetic of the room is simple. A secret held from the messenger is not a secret held from the sender.

**THE SCHOLARS WHO EDITED THE LIGHT**

The tradition of the passage then names the class that made concealment a profession, and the naming is severe. Qatādah reads the preceding charge on the men who heard the word and then altered it after understanding it as the men who heard, comprehended, and changed. Mujāhid goes to the heart of the matter in one sentence: those who used to alter it and conceal its truths were their scholars. The same line of reading is carried by Ibn Zayd, who renders the hearing-and-changing as a work of the desk. The picture is worth holding steady. These were not men who lacked books. They were the men the books were handed to. The alteration named in the passage is the alteration of a text by its own librarians, and the concealment named in this verse is the concealment of the lamp by the lamp-keeper. The decree of the covenant-history keeps the deed in its own words — the words are changed from their places — so that the reader of the two passages together can see the workflow from the oath to the shelf. What follows is exact: the crime of the chamber is not the having of knowledge but the withholding of it from the meeting where it would decide the case.

**THE EYES THAT CLOSE THE LOOP**

The verse's work in the argument is the work of a closing bracket. The passage before it recorded the fear of the leaders that their texts would be used against them. This sentence tells them what the fear itself already proved: the texts are true, the messenger is the man in them, and the concealment is a choice made in the presence of a witness who does not leave the room. The twin statement of the same law in the revelation keeps its doors open on both sides: (3:29 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah.”**). For any age that runs its religion out of a back room — the decision kept from the congregation, the text kept from the reader — the question the verse asks stands unchanged, and its answer does not wait for the judgment of history. The record is made at the whisper. What the leaders revealed in public and buried in private will be read aloud together, and the whole strategy of the closed shelf rests on the one assumption this verse burns: that the room was empty.

---

## Verse 2:78

> And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate

**THE CLASS THE FIRST VERSE LEFT UNNAMED**

The second step of the passage names a class the first verse had left unnamed: ***“And among them are the illiterate”***. The referent is settled by the earliest glosses as the unlearned among the community in question — men who neither read nor write the Scripture — and the lexicographers explain the form as belonging to the family of the mother, as though such a person remained in the state in which his mother bore him, unshaped by the craft of letters. The same designation was worn by the Prophet himself, and the report of the description is transmitted in Bukhārī and Muslim: *"we are an unlettered nation: we do not write and we do not calculate the months"*. That report does double work in the tradition, both marking the Prophet's sign and defining the term as the inability to perform the crafts of the page. A minority reading attached to Ibn ʿAbbās takes the class in a harder direction — a people who accept no prophet and no revealed book, and who write a book of their own and say it is from God, named unlettered for their standing opposition to the Books, which means the label in that reading is earned by stance rather than by schooling — and the majority of the learned hold that reading remote, since in the tongue of the region the designation marks the man who cannot write. The adjudication matters because it decides whether the verse indicts a condition or a policy; the lexical evidence gives the condition, and the next clause supplies the policy.

**THE THREE FACES OF WHAT THEY FOLLOW**

The verse then names the entire intellectual furniture of the class: ***“who know nothing about the Scripture except lies”***. The designation gathered here as lies has been unpacked in three directions across the glosses, and all three are instructive. It means hearsay — the bare report of their leaders, received without knowledge and repeated without examination. It means invention — the manufactured claims of which this passage supplies its own samples, the promise that the Fire will touch them only a counted number of days and the boast that none enters Paradise but their party. And it means wish and desire, the flattering hope that the tongue dresses as scripture. The tradition keeps the double edge of the term in view precisely because its victims believed it as news. The closing verb of the verse then completes the picture: ***“and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate”***. The designation rendered as speculate carries three degrees in the Book's own usage — settled certainty, prevailing likelihood, and bare fancy — and this verse holds the third. One early gloss strips the clause to a single word in the same register as lying; another takes the speculation as the surmise built on what their leaders told them. The point is that conjecture here is not humility before the unknown; it is the confident echo of a fraud, therefore the verse treats the speculation as chargeable rather than forgivable.

**THE TEACHERS STAND FIRST IN THE DOCK**

The hand-off between the two verses carries the passage's deepest judgement of structure, and the narrated analysis states it without softening, because the chain of causation is itself evidence. The superstitiousness of the unlettered was caused; it was manufactured by the dishonesty of men who knew better, and the verse-order keeps the chain visible: the learned are addressed first, the fed are addressed second. What turns on that order is the proportion of guilt. A population raised on pleasing falsehoods is guilty of credulity, since it never checked the hand that fed it, and the men who printed the falsehoods to purchase money and respect with them are guilty of the trade itself. The parallel exposure of distortion in another assembly makes the mechanism explicit — (3:78 — **“There are some among them who distort the Book with their tongues to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is from the Book—but”**) — where the instrument named is the tongue and the product named is confusion about what the Book carries. The educator's duty in every generation follows from the division of the dock, and the reason the passage divides the dock at all is to fix that duty in its order of weight. Those who teach religion answer for what their students quote, because the supply of a pleasing lie is the first act of the crime and the repetition of it by an honest mouth is only the echo. A congregation today that screens its teachers by their receipts rather than their fidelity will find this verse rearranging its hiring practices.

---

## Verse 2:79

> So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned

**A SENTENCE LAID DOWN TWICE**

The verse hands its verdict out in pairs because the crime itself arrived in pairs: ***“So woe to those”***, ***“who distort the Scripture with their own hands”***, ***“then say, “This is from Allah””***, ***“seeking a fleeting gain!”***. The sequence is a forensic file. The hand is named first, because the fabrication was manual — pages rewritten by their custodians — and the glosses on the distortion fix its two chief items: the portrait of the expected prophet in the Torah, redrawn so that it would describe someone else, and the penalty that had stood in the text and was taken out of it. The claim of divine authorship then seals the fraud, and the motive named at the end of the sentence is the smallest item in it: a fleeting gain, the price at which eternity was discounted. The narrations about the trade give the marketplace its floor — fabrications pawned on the unlettered for subsistence money and surplus property — and the whole transaction is what the revelation now bills at full rate. The description they rewrote is the description the revelation restores in public view: (7:157 — **““˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah”**). What follows from the pairing is the passage's arithmetic of guilt: a people were robbed twice over, in their religion and in their wealth, and the sentence counts both takings.

**THE EARNINGS ARRIVE FOR SENTENCE TOO**

The repetition of the woe then turns from the deed to its wage: ***“So woe to them”***, ***“for what their hands have written”***, ***“and woe to them”***, ***“for what they have earned”***. The first count is the fabrication; the second is the fee. The two-faced wrong stands analysed in the tradition with a clarity that needs no amplification: the men disguised the religion of their clients and then took the clients' money for the disguise, which makes the transaction worse than robbery and theft, since the robber takes wealth and leaves religion intact. The doubled woe is therefore the exact shape of the doubled charge, and the smallness of the price is itself part of the judgement. The world entire, from its first day to its last, is a small price; the falsehood these men manufactured became a trap by which they fished the purses of a whole population. The parallel exposure of the same trade in another assembly says the quiet part aloud — (3:78 — **“it is not what the Book says. They say, “It is from Allah”—but it is not from Allah. And ˹so˺”**) — and the sentence inside that passage marks the intent as knowing. For any age that has watched sacred text edited for market share, the verse sets the two ledgers side by side and audits both: the doctrine that was bent and the money that the bending collected.

**THE TERMS OF THE CURSE, OPENED**

The cry of woe itself drew the lexicographers into one of their richest debates, and the debate is worth recording for the weight it puts on the word. The form is a verbal noun with no verb of its own shape, and the definitions gathered around it run from intense evil to sorrow to sheer destruction. Al-Khalil took it as the severity of harm; another lexicographer took it as grief; the wider view holds it as ruin. Al-Asma'i marks the term as an utterance of lamentation, used at times even of pity in the idiom of the language — yet when revelation wields it, the pity is gone and the lament is for the one it lands on. The transmitted glosses from the early generations keep to the plain sense: al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās the definition of the term here as simply *"the chastisement is upon them"*, and a second line of transmission from the same authority renders the woe as a valley of the Fire. A report traced to the first of the successors of the caliphal house has the Prophet define the term as a mountain of the Fire; another, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, pictures it as a valley between two heights into which the falling one tumbles for forty autumns before reaching its floor. The authenticity of that valley-report is itself disputed in the tradition, and some of the learned read the term instead as the very cry the punished will utter. The readings do not cancel one another, because the point is the same in all of them.

**WHERE THE POINTED WORD LANDS**

The proper-name readings and the common-word reading converge on one fact, and the fact is the register of the sentence. Whether the cry names a pit or announces one, it is the heaviest noun the language keeps for such a verdict, and the verse spends it three times. The structure of the passage then does with syntax what the term does with sound: the first woe hangs over the writers, the second over the writing, the third over the wages, and no actor in the chain is left outside the sentence. The judgment follows the paperwork exactly. In other words, the verse is not raining general wrath on a town; it is signing each ledger line with the same name. The effect on a later reader is the effect of reading a bill of particulars, since every clause names a party and every party receives the same currency. A congregation that has learned to treat tampering with scripture as a clerical dispute rather than a crime will find this passage restoring the older scale.

**THE CRY AND THE ACCOUNT IT FOLLOWS**

Read beside the exposure that opened the section, the woe closes a bracket that began with secret pricing. The men who kept two speeches and two inventories now meet a sentence with two counts, and the symmetry is deliberate rather than decorative. What turns on the symmetry is the rule of proportion in the accounting: the punishment fits the paperwork because the paperwork did the harm. The lesson pressed on every later custodian of revelation is therefore exact and practical today: the hand that edits a text for pay signs its own sentence in advance, and the signature is read aloud at the end of the passage in a voice that has never been negotiated with. The pairing of deed and wage is why the passage ends where it does, since a verdict that named only the error would leave the motive unjudged, and the motive is what repeats the crime in every generation.

---

## Verse 2:80

> ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”

**COUNTED DAYS AND THEIR INVENTORIES**

The claim that meets the woe is a claim about arithmetic: ***“˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except”***. The inventories of the counted days differ across the reports, and the differences are themselves informative. One account takes the number as forty, the tally of the days their forefathers worshipped the calf, after which the Fire was promised to cease — Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and others give the figure, and the counting is transparent: forty days of punishment for forty days of apostasy. Another account takes the number as seven, one day for each thousand years of the world's seven thousand, the reckoning reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid in the same shape: the world is seven thousand years, and the torment is one day of the last for each thousand of the first. A third report gives forty years. A fourth detail sharpens the confidence into insult: some held that after their counted term another people would inherit the punishment in their place. The narrated setting of the claim shows the confidence being aired as a taunt — the Prophet asked the gathered community who the people of the Fire were, and they answered that they were, for a while, and that he and his followers would replace them. The clause of counted days in the verse then plays its own grammatical trick: the number is left unnamed because the claimants themselves had fixed it, and the text declines to repeat their arithmetic as though it were worth the ink.

**THE CLAIM'S HIDDEN SCAFFOLDING**

Behind the arithmetic stands a structure of assumptions, and the tradition dismantles it with patience. The claimants reasoned that the law of Moses had not been abrogated, that they were therefore believers, and that a believer's stay in the Fire is a term certain before release. The first assumption is the load-bearing one, and it fails in two places at once: their own book never declared its law eternal, and their denial of the prophets after Moses places them outside the category their argument requires. No scripture of God promises the deniers of His messengers a release after a counted term. The theological principle the argument abuses is real — the books do describe believing offenders as removed from the Fire after their term — but the principle belongs to believers, and the claimants had spent the section proving they were something else. The point is that a true doctrine was pressed into service of a false self-diagnosis, and the verse attacks the diagnosis rather than the doctrine.

**THE PLEDGE NOBODY SIGNED**

The answer then splits the claim into two exhaustive branches: ***“for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah”***, ***“for Allah never breaks His word”***. The dilemma is built in the tradition with old precision: either the claimants hold a covenant from their Lord, in which case the claim stands and the covenant holds; or they are saying about God what they do not know, in which case the claim is invention and the inventors have assigned terms to their Lord without a text. The known history of the claimants settles which branch they stand on, since a people who belied prophet after prophet hold no signed pledge, and the second branch closes over them. The middle clause about God never breaking His word is then doing quiet work. It concedes the fidelity of God in order to remove the last shelter of the claim: fidelity to a promise cannot manufacture a promise that was never made. The parallel statement of the same claim elsewhere in the Book labels its psychology without ceremony — (3:24 — **“for a few days.” They have been deceived in their faith by their wishful lying”**) — and the counterweight of the general law stands where the law states it: (4:93 — **“And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell—where they will stay indefinitely. Allah will be displeased with them,”**).

**PROMISE AND PERMISSION KEPT APART**

The passage, read whole, governs a question the tradition treats with unusual care, and the care is visible in a threefold distinction. First, the verse rebukes the confident figure flung without a promise, not the bare possibility of a believing sinner's release after a term; the indignation attaches to the invented number and the insolence of its confidence. Second, no general amnesty is assumed for a whole population; the books describe individual forgiveness, not demographic exemptions. Third — and this is the hinge — there is a difference between saying that God will not remove a believing offender and saying that God never promised to remove one. What turns on that difference is the whole space of hope: the absence of a promise is not the absence of an act, and the Lord of the affair acts by wisdom even where He has published no terms. The verse therefore disciplines the tongue rather than the doctrine, since the doctrine of divine mercy stands untouched and the claim of automatic tenure falls.

**THE DEMAND THE QUESTION MAKES**

The interrogative that answers the claim has two horns and no third: ***“or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?””***. The tradition states the logic in one line — the truth of their claim depends on one of two matters with no third available — and the sentence then leaves the claimants holding either a document or a fabrication. The practical demand this places on every later audience is exactly the demand the verse models. Religious promises of automatic amnesty are claims about the afterlife's contract law, and the verse teaches the only admissible procedure: produce the pledge in its text, or withdraw the claim and return to hope joined to works. The covenant they were actually given says something else entirely, since the pledge on record is a moral one they broke rather than a demographic guarantee they hold: (2:84 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes,”**). The effect of the question is procedural, because it converts a slogan into a citation request. In other words, the passage does not trade insult with the claim; it asks for the signature, and silence answers for the claimants. A community today that markets guarantees the books never issued will find this passage asking for the signature first.

---

## Verse 2:81

> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**A PARTICLE THAT TURNS THE VERDICT**

One particle turns the whole passage over, and the grammarians made it a study text: ***“But no! Those who commit evil”***. The cry of certainty that opens the verse answers the claim that closed the last one, and the form of the answer was argued with the precision the question deserved. Sibawayh held that this particle and its affirmative twin are not nouns but particles like the simpler turn of correction, and the verse's usage here is a reply to the saying that the Fire would touch them only for counted days. The Kufan analysts read the form as that simpler turn with a euphonic letter added for the pause, the added letter carrying an affirmation inside it: the one particle negates a negation and the other affirms what was negated. The effect is surgical, because the claim was itself a negation — the Fire will not touch us — and this answer both cancels the cancellation and installs the opposite. The tradition presses the logic further: the universal statement stands as the major premise of a syllogism whose minor clause is left out, and the elision is more eloquent than spelling it would be. The point of the construction is that a claim about time is answered with a claim about character, since days can be granted by concession but character cannot be granted at all. What follows is therefore not a competing arithmetic of days but a law of persons, and the law states itself once for everyone in the same sentence. The book of the covenant's own summary puts the same rule in contract form — (98:6 — **“Indeed, those who disbelieve from the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell,”**) — notice who is named in it: membership buys no quota.

**WHAT SURROUNDS THE SOUL AT ITS END**

The verse then describes the condition of the condemned: ***“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”***. The middle phrase is a picture of geometry as much as morality, and the early generations read the surrounding three ways that nearly converge. One reading, transmitted by Abū Hurayrah and others, takes the surrounding as associationism itself: the idolatry wraps the person as a wrapper encloses its content. A second, from al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym through the teachers of Kufah and shared by al-Suddī, takes it as the state of one who dies without repenting, the wrongs closing over the record before it is opened. A third, held by Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Hasan, and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas among others, takes it as the major sins that master their doer. The difference between the three readings is slight in practice, since each describes the same final posture of the soul from a different angle. The Arabic verb itself can mean to encircle, to enclose, or to comprehend, and the picture the glosses share is spatial: sin becomes the outer wall of the self, so that whatever good remains is inside the wrong rather than the wrong inside the good. In other words, the question at the end is not how long the record is but which side of the self the record sits on. A line of transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās through one of his students puts the whole reading in one report: *"whoever does what you did and disbelieves as you disbelieved until his unbelief surrounds whatever good he had — those are the companions of the Fire, they will abide therein forever"*. The companion report about accumulation, transmitted by Ibn Masʿūd with the collection of Aḥmad, agrees: when small sins gather, they bring about destruction. The last word of the verse then does the work the whole exchange demanded. Where the claim counted days, the verdict says forever, and the covenant-mountain passage had already ruled that the term is not up to the claimants: (11:108 — **“and the earth will endure, except what your Lord wills—a ˹generous˺ giving, without end”**). This is why the verse can close with a single word: the word carries the weight of a whole calendar. For a modern reader who keeps a private ledger of tolerable offences, the passage answers with the physics of the soul rather than a toll: what surrounds you at the end is what you built.

---

## Verse 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

**THE VERSE THAT MUST STAND BESIDE IT**

The promise that answers the threat is written in the same shape, and the pairing is the pedagogy: ***“And those who believe”***, ***“and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever”***. The early analysts of the sequence note the wisdom in the alternation — the promise is sweetened with the threat and the threat with the promise, so that the warning grows by mention of what its people forfeit of reward, and the promise grows by mention of what its people escape of punishment. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the first clause as belief in the Messenger and the revelation, and the second as acts of obedience between the servant and his Lord; the closing words he reads as perpetuity without death and without exit, the exact mirror of the Fire's own perpetuity. The symmetry is the point. Two destinies are stated in two sentences of identical architecture, so that the reader cannot extract the amnesty-half of the passage and file it alone. The composition itself disciplines the reader's eye: the two verdicts share a verb tense and a duration, and only their populations differ. Where the previous verse closed the door on a demographic exemption, this one opens the door on an individual covenant, and the covenant has two named terms and no third.

**TWO HINGES AND THE DOOR**

The grammar of the pair drew the language specialists more than once, because the second clause is coordinated onto the first rather than absorbed into it. A part is not coordinated onto a whole; if works were already inside the name of belief, the coordination would be tautology. The arrangement therefore marks two things in order: the assent of the heart and the fruit the assent bears. The glosses make the same point functionally — belief in God and His Messenger, then the deeds that conform to the revealed law — and the tradition of the doctrine adds the reason the unrepentant cannot claim the first term without the second. Faith is itself the greatest good in an account, so a believer's ledger can never be empty of goodness however thin the entries; and minor wrongs are absorbed in forgiveness unless obstinacy promotes them, which is why the surrounding-sentence of the last verse cannot land on this people. The reason the two terms travel together is now visible: the first without the second is assent without its fruit, and the second without the first is labor without its ground. The twin verdict in the other assembly of the same theme says it flatly — (98:7 — **“Indeed, those who believe and do good—they are the best of ˹all˺ beings”**) — and the reward-language of the covenant-curse keeps the individual ledger in view. What turns on the pairing is the whole shape of hope: entry is by faith and good work together, and the two terms are not rival claimants but one road with two feet.

**THE RULE BENEATH THE WHOLE CLAIM**

The closing of this argument is worth reading in its full severity, because it withdraws the assumption beneath the entire claim of counted days. Grace is not parceled by wishes or by ancestry; the reckoning runs on deeds and their doers: (4:123 — **“˹Divine grace is˺ neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book! Whoever commits evil will be rewarded accordingly,”**). The passage therefore settles what the whole exchange had circled: the judgment follows the individual's works, not the family's papers, and no community carries a standing exemption written into the terms. The early doctrine states the effect plainly — the denial of the later prophets put the claimants outside the covenant their argument needed, and the promise of release stands beside the works, not beside the bloodline. That is why the claim of the earlier verses had to be met with a question about a pledge rather than a counter-number. The difference the verse presses on every later audience today is the difference between inherited religion and practiced religion: the first assumes the covenant, the second keeps it. In other words, the door to the Garden is hung on two hinges, faith and work, and the passage that began with an invented amnesty closes by showing the only lease that holds.

---

## Verse 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent

**THE SEVEN TERMS OF THE FIRST PLEDGE**

The covenant is recalled in its Torah form, and the list it carries is a constitution in miniature: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none”***, ***“but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans”***. The first term is God's own right, and the glosses define its content as three duties in one: affirm the unity, attest the messengers, and act by the books. This is the foundation, the ethicists of the tradition say, without which no other work is accepted. The second term is the first of the creatures' rights, and the arrangement itself is the teaching. The books mention the rights of parents beside the rights of God, so that gratitude to the two is named in one breath: (17:23 — **“For your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him. And honour your parents.”**). The Arabic phrase for the second term is strikingly spare. Its surface sense is and toward parents virtue, the verb understood rather than written, and the grammar of the ellipsis was noted as an understood command. What follows walks outward in circles: the kin whose name in Arabic means the possessors of nearness, then the orphans whose definition in the juridical handbooks is the minor who lost the father who provided, then the needy named in almost every passage where relatives and orphans are named. The sequence is a lesson in the sociology of obligation. Worship begins at the altar and ends at the street.

**THE COURTESY THAT TRUTHFULNESS REQUIRES**

The fourth term is speech, and the verse grants it the same expansion the others received: ***“and the needy”***, ***“speak kindly to people”***, ***“establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.””***. The kind word in this covenant is not decoration. The glosses unpack it as commanding right and forbidding wrong while staying truthful about the status of the awaited prophet, with kindness in act toward the orphan and the poor. The manners clause was pressed into service in a scene the tradition keeps for its tone. When a student complained to ʿAṭāʾ of his own harshness toward people of unsound doctrine and said he dealt with them roughly, the scholar pointed him back to the kind words this verse prescribes and answered: *"Allah has commanded us to speak to people politely. When Jews and Christians all are to be treated like this, would this commandment not apply to a Muslim?"* The pedagogy of the prophets is the same. The books record Moses and Aaron sent to the worst tyrant of their age with instructions to use gentle words. The tone of any modern caller to any faith is therefore a doctrinal matter and not a trait of personality. Prayer and the alms-tax then close the list. The vertical covenant carries its social dividend, the five daily meetings and the share that keeps the poor inside the community's arithmetic. The list as a whole refuses to separate what it joins. Theology is followed immediately by parents, and worship immediately by wages, because the covenant contracts for both tables at once.

**ORDINANCES THAT CARRY NO EXPIRY**

The doctrine that emerges from the list is a doctrine of permanence. These ordinances are the principles of religion that every revealed law has commanded, since they answer the general interests of every time and place, and the means to a favor is itself a favor. The tradition therefore treats them as un-abrogated in substance even where the specific statutes of earlier laws were replaced, and the catalogue keeps reappearing in the later surahs in nearly the same order. The ranking of deeds inside the covenant was shown in the report the two major collections record from Ibn Masʿūd: *"I asked the Messenger of Allah which action is best. He said: Prayer at its proper time. I said: Then which? He said: Goodness to parents. I said: Then which? He said: Jihad in the cause of Allah."* Two of the three answers stand inside the verse's own list. The breach is then stated in the verse's own tense — ***“But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away”***, ***“except for a few of you”***, ***“and were indifferent”*** — and the addressing of descendants in the second person is part of the passage's forensic style. The third-person reading makes the sentence a plain historical report. The second-person reading makes the covenant a standing summons that every generation must sign or breach. The few who refused the turning-away were identified in the earliest glosses by name, the converts of the first hour from among the scholars of the community. The indifference of the majority is the measure of what the pledge was worth in practice.

**THE OATH THE TEXT ATTACHES ITSELF TO**

One grammatical detail from the legal language of the covenant deserves recording, because it shows how seriously the form was argued. The commandment stands as if attached to an oath, and Sibawayh's analysis of the syntax turns the list itself into sworn testimony rather than counsel. A covenant here takes its name from the root of binding with an oath, the kind of assurance that secures a promise against the promiser's temper. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same definition: the pledge taken is a pledge secured by oath. The hardness that required such forms was itself noted in the tradition. A people who resisted every plain command until they were met with fearful oaths have revealed, by the manner of their binding, the manner of their turning. The judgment this passage performs is therefore not a surprise inspection but a contract trial. The trial file carries the document the signatories themselves signed. For any later house that treats its founding covenant as heirloom rather than obligation, the closing words of the verse remain the sharpest commentary. The pledge is still in force, the signature is still legible, and the indifference is still counted.

---

## Verse 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness

**THE ARTICLE THEY KEPT AND THE TWO THEY BROKE**

The second article of the pledge is civil, and its terms read like a statute: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant”***, ***“that you would neither shed each other’s blood”***. The glosses fix the range of the clause at once. The forbidden shedding is the spilling of one another's blood, kinsman and ally alike. The first named witnesses of the tradition point to the two clans whose houses the later fighting emptied as the clause's standing examples. The figure in the wording was itself dissected. Killing another member of the community is called killing oneself, since the blood is joined to the shedder by kin or by religion or by the retaliation it unleashes. A second reading hears a warning about consequence: do not spill others' blood so that your own is spilled, as though you had shed it yourself. A third hears a plea against the deeds that make blood lawful at all. The scale of the crime is set elsewhere in the book in the terms the covenant only implies: (5:32 — **“That is why We ordained for the Children of Israel that whoever takes a life—unless as a punishment for”**). The prohibition is not a courtesy of the sanctuary. It is the first law of the commonwealth.

**THE WAR THE COVENANT WAS WRITTEN AGAINST**

The historical setting is given with unusual care, and it makes the covenant's teeth visible. The two clans of the city had fought their old wars under the alliance system of the age of ignorance. Three Jewish factions had each allied with one of the warring parties. When the battle lines met, a man would fight beside his ally against fighters who included members of his own people. When the war ended, the victors ransomed the captives of their own side. The tradition marks that whole arrangement as the background of the charge, and the ethicists of the revelation put the arithmetic in plain terms. Three obligations stood together in the covenant: do not shed one another's blood, do not expel one another from your homes, and ransom your captive. The community acted on the third while breaking the first two. The perversity of that selective observance is the whole accusation. The article they kept was the article that cost them least after the fighting was already over. The expulsion clause widened the civil protection. It forbade the harassment that drives a household out without any decree, and the line from Ibn ʿAbbās names the houses the practice emptied before the sentence arrived.

**THE SIGNATURE THE SIGNATORIES GAVE AWAY**

The covenant closes on a clause about testimony, and the clause is the passage's quiet masterpiece: ***“nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge”***, ***“and bore witness”***. The agreement is described in the glosses as explicit as the statement of a witness in court. To confirm the pledge is to accept it as true and binding. To bear witness is to attest it against oneself in the very act of acceptance. One line of reading hears the clause as addressed to the community in the present tense: you confess the acceptance even now, as the sentence is read over you. Another line takes it as the plain fact of the first assent. They ratified it while knowing exactly what they were doing, and the tradition keeps that reading from Ibn ʿAbbās in its bluntest form. The parallel summons of the scripture-bearers elsewhere draws the same portrait from life: (3:187 — **“and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain. What a miserable profit”**). Together the two passages define the crime as a knowing breach and not a lapse of memory. What turns on the witness-language is the legal position of the house at the bar. The covenant is not being alleged. It is being produced with the defendant's own signature on it.

**THE SELF THE VERSE CALLS THE VICTIM**

The deepest reading of the clause is the one the wording invites, and it survives every historical setting the passage has been read through. The members are joined into one self by confession and kin, so the shedding of the brother is the wounding of the body and the expulsion of the neighbor is the flight of the limb from its own trunk. The doctrine that the faithful are like a single body, each member answering for the rest, is the anthropology this grammar assumes. It is why the verse can address a whole nation as one witness who perjured himself. The reason the grammar matters is that it turns a moral appeal into a legal fact. A body cannot un-own its limb, and a nation cannot un-sign its charter. The practical consequence for a modern community that reads its charter in the mirror is exact. A covenant signed in public is enforced in public, and the testimony that once blessed the signature will also testify to the breach. The verse ends where every court ends, with the party's own words.

---

## Verse 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do

**A FIGHT FOUGHT FOR THE ALLY'S HONOR**

The opening pronoun of reproach was analyzed for its own grammar, because the shape of the address carries the accusation: ***“But here you are, killing each other”***, ***“and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin”***. The particle that introduces the sentence marks estrangement in the very occurrence and not delay in time. The thing is happening, and its happening is the shock. The emphatic pronoun places the house in the dock as its own defendant. The verb of mutual assistance carries an assimilated spelling and an unassimilated variant, and its range is the range of the charge. It means helping one another against them in sin, and the glosses split the sin into disobedience toward God and injustice toward people. The crime is thus an infringement of two rights at once: the right of God broken in the defiance, and the right of creatures broken in the pain. The geometry of the scene is what makes it infamous. Men of one household fought under the flag of a foreign ally against members of their own household, then returned to empty the houses of their own kin. The passage does not describe a war between religions. It describes a war in which religion was the loot.

**THE PARANTHESIS THE STATUTE HIDES**

The middle of the verse is built like a legal instrument, and the language specialists found its joints worth mapping: ***“and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you”***, ***“as captives, you still ransom them”***, ***“though expelling them was unlawful”***. The ransoming clause comes with two reading variants in the consonantal tradition, one on the captives and one on the act of delivering them with money. The glosses stress that this ransoming was itself one of the pledged articles. The forbidden-expulsion clause is then tied grammatically back to the expulsion verb, with the ransoming statement sitting between them as a parenthesis. The statute forbade the expulsion in exactly the same way it forbade abandoning the ransom. The practice's own logic is preserved in the tradition in the form of the questions the practitioners were asked. When they were asked why they fought men and then paid for their release, they answered that ransoming was commanded. When they were asked why they fought at all, they answered that they feared the humiliation of their allies. The exchange is the whole moral picture in miniature: piety in the account books, and honor in the battle line. The pattern of listening to scripture only when it speaks conveniently is drawn to the same scale elsewhere in the revelation: (4:46 — **“Some Jews take words out of context and say, “We listen and we disobey,” “Hear! May you never hear,””**).

**THE ALLIANCE MAP BEHIND THE CHARGE**

The historical map is given in the tradition with names, and it turns the general charge into a courtroom exhibit. The city's two clans had fought their old wars of the age of ignorance, and three Jewish factions had entered the alliance system. One faction allied to one clan, one to the other, and one held kinship with both. When the alliances flipped across generations, the combat itself crossed the community's own bloodlines. The men of one faction would fight beside their patrons against fighters who included their own people. They would kill their own and empty their homes at the rout. They would then buy back the prisoners of their own side when the fighting stopped. The disgrace this worldly life promised them is recorded in the tradition as having landed in their own later history in the form the sentence prescribes. A clan was slain after its allies had marched on it, and a clan was marched out of its houses into exile with the tax of submission imposed on the remainder. The particle of the sequence therefore does rhetorical work beyond chronology. It says: and it is you, of all people, who do this. For a house that reads the passage now, the alliance map is the warning against the oldest habit of party spirit: arranging the faith around the patron and then billing the faith for the war.

**THE HALF-BELIEF THE QUESTION NAMES**

The indictment then rises from the deed to the doctrine the deed implied: ***“for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture”***, ***“and reject the rest?”***. The earliest glosses hear two charges in the question, and both stand. In the specific register, the believers-in-part are those who kept the article commanding the ransom of captives while discarding the articles that forbade the killing, the expulsion, and the alliance-assistance. This is a docket of observance chosen by convenience. In the general register, the question names the whole method of taking from the book what suits the whim and leaving what rebukes it. The structure of the accusation is the one the final revelation states as a creed, where the faithful define themselves by refusing the selection altogether: (2:285 — **“and His messengers. ˹They proclaim,˺ “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.” And they say, “We hear”**). What follows from the pairing is the doctrine of the book as an indivisible trust. To believe part and reject part is not a lesser belief. It is a different religion wearing the first one's vocabulary. The judgment this passage performs is therefore not on ignorance but on the editor's pen, the same pen the earlier woe already priced.

**TWO FLOORS OF DISGRACE**

The sentence of the verse is then set on two floors, and the architecture of the punishment is deliberate: ***“Is there any reward”***, ***“for those who do”***, ***“so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life”***. The first floor is historical. The earliest glosses read the worldly disgrace as killing and captivity, the community paying for its selective practice in the currency it had minted. The men who ransomed prisoners of war by the book were led away as prisoners themselves. The second floor is jurisprudential, and the pairing with the first is the point. The disgrace of history answers the disgrace of doctrine, so that the public shame is the visible form of the inner break. The comparative in the verse's second floor, the punishment named as the most severe, was read by the language specialists as the elative form doing superlative work. It is not merely severe. It is the severe itself. The structure echoes the doubled sentence of the writing-verse earlier in the passage, where the deed and its wage each received their own woe. Here the world and the last day each receive their own disgrace.

**THE WATCH THAT KEEPS THE FULL ACCOUNT**

The close answers the practice's hidden theory with one sentence: ***“and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?”***, ***“For Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. The hidden theory of selective observance is always the theory of the unwatched ledger: that the unobserved articles cost nothing and the unexamined motives weigh nothing. The assurance of the verse withdraws the theory at its root, and the transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās states the refusal of the discount plainly: *"He is not reducing your punishment because of what you do"* — and the same authority adds the second register, that the accounting also covers what was concealed. The chain of readings on the final verb keeps both parties in view. Whether the sentence reads that He is not heedless of what you do or of what they do, the reach of the watch is the same. The effect on a modern congregation is procedural rather than spectacular. A house today that keeps its charter's comfortable articles and files away the costly ones is standing in exactly this dock, and the closing line is the court's assurance that every article is on the books.

---

## Verse 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped

**THE TRADE THE VERDICT NAMES**

The verse reduces the whole preceding file to a single transaction: ***“These are the ones”***, ***“who trade the Hereafter”***, ***“for the life of this world.”***. The glosses define the exchange without sentiment: purchasing the present life at the price of the next by preferring the first to the second. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās pairs the columns by kind — this lower world in place of the world to come, and disbelief in place of belief. The commerce vocabulary is doing the work of a whole theology of value, because a trade names two goods and their agreed rates, and the verse's accusation is not that the men pursued the world but that they priced eternity at the world's rate. The earlier woe had already called the price small and the gain fleeting; the present verse removes even the appearance of shrewdness from the deal, since the merchandise forfeited is named in its full weight before the sentence names the buyers. The books elsewhere draw the same transaction from the other side, where the bargain is written as it should be written — (4:74 — **“Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. And whoever fights in Allah’s cause—whether”**) — and the difference between the two passages is the difference between a purchase and a sale. In other words, the same exchange runs in two directions: the faithful trade this life for the next, and the men of this verse trade the next for this one.
